Ya'qub first fought Kharijites in Sistan, and in 865 he defeated and killed their leader Ammar ibn Yaser. His armies took Kabul and Bamiyan from the Hindu Shahis, and by 870 the whole of Khorasan was under his control. In 867 he sent the caliph al-Mu'tazz a poem claiming the inheritance of the kings of Persia. In 873 he ousted the Tahirids from Nishapur and captured their ruler Muhammad ibn Tahir, which led to conflict with the Abbasid caliphate. He took Fars in 875.

In 876 al-Muwaffaq offered him the governorship of Khurasan, Tabaristan, Fars, Gurgan and Ray; Ya'qub refused and advanced towards Baghdad. The armies met at Dayr al-Aqul on 8 April 876. His troops numbered about ten thousand, and the Abbasids were superior in numbers. The Saffarid army, somewhat reluctant to fight the caliph, broke and fled, and many men drowned in flooded land. Ya'qub withdrew from Iraq.

Ya'qub suffered from colic and refused treatment. He died at Gundeshapur on 5 June 879, and his brother Amr succeeded him. Accounts of his religion differ: some sources call him a Kharijite, a Christian or an Ismaili, while the historian D. G. Tor presents evidence that he was a devout Sunni warrior. During his rule Persian was introduced as an official language, and he reportedly did not know Arabic. He has the status of a popular folk hero because his court revived the Persian language, and poets traced his genealogy to the Iranian king Jamshid of tradition. His campaigns also marked an early stage in the decline of caliphal political unity.
yaqub-ibn-killis: Abu'l-Faraj Ya'qub ibn Yusuf ibn Killis was born in Baghdad into a Jewish family. He came to Egypt as a young man, in 943 according to one account, and entered the service of Kafur, the power behind the Ikhshidid regime, where he rose as an expert in finance and took charge of the household and property. He converted to Islam in 967, which pleased Kafur but roused the jealousy of the vizier Ibn al-Furat. When Kafur died in 968 Ibn al-Furat arrested his companions; Ya'qub, it is said, bribed his jailer and escaped to Ifriqiya, where he entered the service of the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz.

Al-Mu'izz gave him charge of the economy. After the Fatimid conquest of Egypt in 969 he went there, by one account with Jawhar as-Siqilli and by another with the caliph in 972, and when Ibn al-Furat resigned in 974 the administration passed to him. Under al-Aziz he became chief minister, Wazir al-Adjall, a title the earlier Fatimid caliphs' assistants had not borne. He set up departments of state anew, promoted agriculture, reformed trade and stabilised the currency, and the treasury was fuller than ever before. In 983/4 he fell from favour and was fined 20,000 gold dinars for reasons unknown, but within months he was back in office.

He was also a scholar who lectured at his palace every Friday night to judges, theologians, grammarians and poets, and a work on theology compiled with 40 theologians, the Risalat al-Waziria, is attributed to him. His annual income was put at 100,000 dinars, and he kept a private force of 4,000 young men.

He fell seriously ill on 10 January 991, and al-Aziz, visiting him, offered to give away the state's wealth or his own son for his recovery. He died on 22 February 991 and was mourned throughout Egypt. According to Ibn Khallikan, 100 poets composed laments for him, each rewarded by the caliph, and a district of Cairo was named the Vizier's Quarter in his honour.
yaqui: The Yaqui call themselves Hiaki or Yoeme, their word for person, and their homeland Hiakim. They speak Yaqui, or Yoem Noki, a Cahitan language of the Uto-Aztecan family spoken by about 16,000 people. When the Spanish first met them in 1533 they numbered an estimated 30,000 people in 80 villages along the lower Yaqui River, most of them farming beans, maize and squash on land the river flooded each year, while others fished near its mouth or hunted and gathered in the deserts and mountains.

After defeating the Spanish in two battles in 1608 and making peace in 1610, the Yaqui invited Jesuit missionaries in 1617. Over some 120 years most converted to Christianity while keeping many traditional beliefs, and the Jesuits gathered them into eight towns, among them Vícam, Pótam and Tórim. Encroachment on their land led to a revolt with the Mayo in 1740 in which one thousand Spanish and 5,000 Native Americans were killed.

After Mexican independence the Yaqui refused to pay taxes. Juan Banderas led a revolt in 1825 and was executed in 1833, and Cajemé led the struggle until his execution in 1887; in 1868 the army burned 150 Yaqui to death inside a church. By 1908 at least 5,000 Yaqui had been sold into slavery on plantations, where most died, two thirds within a year of arriving. The last major battle was fought at Cerro del Gallo in 1927. In 1937 President Lázaro Cárdenas reserved 500,000 hectares of ancestral land on the river's north bank and ordered a dam built for irrigation.

Today there are eight Yaqui pueblos in Sonora. Yaqui who fled the violence formed the Pascua Yaqui Tribe of Arizona, based in Tucson, which received 817,000 square metres of land in 1964 and federal recognition on 18 September 1978.

Many Yoeme hold that the universe is made of overlapping worlds, the aniam, such as the flower world and the wilderness world. The deer dance, accompanied by the deer song, joins three of them, and many believe the world depends on their yearly Lenten and Easter rituals. Flowers, held to have sprung from the blood shed at the crucifixion, are seen as the manifestation of souls.
yaqut-al-hamawi: Yaqut, meaning ruby or hyacinth, was the kunya of Ibn Abdullah, "son of Abdullah". He was born in Constantinople, the Byzantine capital called al-Rum in Arabic, whence his nisba al-Rumi. Captured in war and enslaved, he became the mawali of Askar ibn Abi Nasr al-Hamawi, a trader of Baghdad, from whom he received the laqab al-Hamawi. As Askar's apprentice he learned accounting and commerce and travelled as his envoy, twice or three times, to Kish in the Persian Gulf. In 1194 Askar stopped his salary over some dispute, and Yaqut worked as a copyist and studied under the grammarian al-Ukbari. Five years later he made another mission to Kish for Askar.

On his return to Baghdad Yaqut set up as a bookseller and began to write. He then spent ten years travelling in Iran, Syria and Egypt. His importance as a scholar lies in his testimony to the great, largely lost literary heritage held in libraries east of the Caspian Sea, since he was one of the last visitors before the Mongol invaders destroyed them. He gained much material from the libraries of Merv, where he had studied for two years, and of Balkh. About 1222 he was working on his Geography in Mosul and he completed the first draft in 1224. In 1227 he was in Alexandria, and he moved from there to Aleppo, where he died in 1229.

The Mu'jam al-Buldan, "Dictionary of Countries", was composed between 1224 and 1228 and completed a year before his death. It is classed as a literary geography: an alphabetical index of place names from the literary corpus of the Arabs, with their vocalisations, their Arabic or foreign derivation and their location. Yaqut supplements the geographic descriptions with historical and ethnographic material, accounts of Muslim conquests, names of governors, monuments and local celebrities, and so preserves much early literary, historical, biographical and geographic material, in prose and poetry.

His Mu'jam al-Udaba, the "Literary Encyclopedia" of 1226, is also known as the Irshad al-Arib. Another work, al-Mushtarak, is a lexicon of geographical homonyms, edited by Ferdinand Wüstenfeld in 1846. Wüstenfeld also edited the Mu'jam al-Buldan in six volumes, published at Leipzig.
yarim-lim-i: Yarim-Lim, also written Yarimlim, was the second king of the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad, the son of its first king Sumu-Epuh and his queen Sumunna-Abi. He came to the throne at a time of danger: Shamshi-Adad I of the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia had surrounded Yamhad through alliances with Carchemish and Urshu to the north and Qatna to the south, and had conquered Mari to the east, placing his son Yasmah-Adad on its throne. Sumu-Epuh was killed campaigning against him. Yarim-Lim's wife was Gashera, whose parents are unknown, and their daughter Shibtu married Zimri-Lim of Mari.

Yarim-Lim held out against Shamshi-Adad. Around 1777 BCE he conquered the city of Tuttul, and when Shamshi-Adad died around 1776 BCE he helped Zimri-Lim, the heir of Mari, drive out Yasmah-Adad and take the throne. Zimri-Lim called him father and acted under the guidance of Hadad, the chief god of Yamhad, whose mediator Yarim-Lim was. The tablets of Mari show this dependence: Yarim-Lim refused to hand over men Zimri-Lim asked for, giving way only at the Mari ambassador's third request, and Zimri-Lim turned down a peace offer from Ibal-pi-el II of Eshnunna three times when Aleppo withheld its consent.

Ibal-pi-el later allied with Elam, the enemy of Yarim-Lim's ally Hammurabi of Babylon. Yarim-Lim's influence reached Ugarit, and his armies campaigned as far as Elam. A tablet found at Mari holds his declaration of war on Dēr and Diniktum, reminding the king of Dēr that Yarim-Lim had given him military help for 15 years and had kept 500 warships of Aleppo at Diniktum for 12 years.

Yarim-Lim died around 1764 BCE and was succeeded by his son Hammurabi I. His widow Gashera outlived him and remained a strong-willed figure in the politics of the kingdom after his death. The historian William Hamblin called Yarim-Lim at the height of his power "the mightiest ruler in the Near East outside of Egypt".
yarkand: Yarkand, or Yarkant County, lies on the southern rim of the Taklamakan Desert in the Tarim Basin, at an altitude of 1,189 metres, and is administered under Kashgar Prefecture. The oasis is fed by the Yarkand River, which flows north from the Karakorum and through the Kunlun Mountains. It now covers 3,210 square kilometres but was probably far more extensive before a period of desiccation that began from the 3rd century CE. The oasis farmland produces cotton, wheat, corn, pomegranates, pears, apricots and walnuts.

The Book of Han of the 1st century BCE first mentions the territory as Shaju, probably related to the name of the Iranian Saka tribes. In the 1st century CE the kingdom of Suoju was the most powerful in the Western Regions. Its king Xian, given the seal of Protector General in 41 CE and then denied it, conquered Kucha and other kingdoms, until Guangde of Khotan captured him in 61 CE and killed him. The Han general Ban Chao defeated Suoju in 86 CE, and in 130 CE Yarkand sent tribute to the Chinese emperor along with Ferghana and Kashgar.

Little is recorded for many centuries after that. Yarkant became the main base of Chagatai Khan, who inherited Kashgaria after Genghis Khan died in 1227. Marco Polo described it in 1273 as a province where people followed the law of Mahomet, with some Nestorian Christians, and rich in cotton. In 1509 the Dughlats rebelled against Moghulistan, and five years later Sultan Said Khan conquered them and set up the Yarkent Khanate, with Yarkand as its capital. The Jesuit Benedict Göez reached the city in 1603 and called it a mart of much note, where the Kabul caravan ended and a new one formed for Cathay.

The Qing dynasty gained control of the region in the middle of the 18th century. By the 19th century trade with Ladakh and foreign merchants made it the largest and most populous state of Kashgar. In the 1860s Yakub Beg made Yarkant the capital of his Turkic state of Yettishar and received embassies from England in 1870 and 1873. The Qing defeated him in 1877, and he committed suicide. Yarkant is now predominantly Uyghur, with a small Tajik minority.
yarkent-khanate: The Yarkent Khanate, also called the Yarkand Khanate and the Kashghar Khanate, was a Sunni Muslim khanate ruled by Turkified Mongol descendants of Chagatai Khan, son of Genghis Khan. Its ruling house belonged to the Eastern Chaghatayid, or Moghul, dynasty. The Chagatai Khanate collapsed in the first half of the 14th century. Its western part became the Empire of Timur in 1370, and its eastern part became Moghulistan, created by Tughluk Timur Khan in 1347 with its capital at Almalik, in the Ili River Valley. Moghulistan comprised the settled lands of eastern Kashgaria and the regions of Turpan and Kumul.

The Dughlats had ruled Kashgaria as vassals since 1220, when Chagatai Khan granted them most of it. In 1509 they rebelled against Moghulistan. Sultan Said Khan, a brother of the Khan of Eastern Moghulistan, or the Turpan Khanate, then conquered them, took Kashgar, Yarkent and Hotan from Mirza Abu Bakr Dughlat and set up his own khanate. Yarkent was its capital until its fall in 1705, as it had been for the Dughlat state.

The khanate was predominantly Uyghur and Turki, and its populous cities included Hotan, Yarkent, Kashgar, Yangihissar, Aksu, Kucha, Karashar, Turpan and Kumul. Its conquest of the Dughlats ended their dominance in Kashgaria and made it the foremost power of the region. Said Khan's reign was heavily influenced by the khojas, and he had a close relationship with his cousin Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire. He campaigned in Bolor in 1527 to 1528, raided Badakhshan in 1529, and led looting expeditions into Ladakh and Kashmir in 1532. He reportedly died in 1533 at Daulat Beg Oldi of high-altitude pulmonary edema while returning from Ladakh and Kashmir.

His successor Abdurashid Khan, who ruled from 1533 to 1565, began by executing a member of the Dughlat family. He fought the Kirghiz and the Kazakhs for control of western Moghulistan, which was ultimately lost, so that the Moghuls were largely restricted to the Tarim Basin. The khanate enjoyed dominance in the region for about 200 years, until the Buddhist Dzungar Khanate conquered Altishahr from 1678 to 1705, and Tsewang Rabtan took the khanate in 1705.
yarlung-tsangpo: The Yarlung Tsangpo, also called Yarlung Zangbo (Chinese Yalu Zangbu Jiang), is the upper course of the Brahmaputra. It flows through the Tibet Autonomous Region of China and Arunachal Pradesh in India, and it is the longest river of Tibet. Its upper section is also called Dangque Zangbu, meaning Horse River. It rises at the Angsi Glacier in western Tibet, southeast of Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, and then forms the South Tibet Valley, which is about 1,200 kilometres long and 300 kilometres wide. The valley descends from 4,500 metres to 3,000 metres above sea level, and the vegetation changes from cold desert to arid steppe, deciduous scrub, and finally conifer and rhododendron forest.

The river's basin lies between the Himalayas in the south and the Kang Rinpoche and Nyenchen Tanglha mountains in the north. Its climate is less severe than that of the higher parts of northern Tibet, and the basin is home to most of the population of the Tibet Autonomous Region. Where the river leaves the Tibetan Plateau it bends around Namcha Barwa in a horseshoe and forms the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, the deepest and possibly the longest canyon in the world. It then enters Arunachal Pradesh, where it widens and is called the Siang, and in Assam it becomes the Brahmaputra.

The river has three major waterfalls. The largest, the Hidden Falls, became known in the West in 1998, when its sighting was briefly hailed as a discovery, although Tibetan hunters and Buddhist monks had told stories of the great falls. Chinese authorities replied that Chinese geographers, exploring the gorge since 1973, had already photographed the falls from a helicopter in 1987. Since the 1990s kayaking teams have attempted the river. A Japanese group lost a member in 1993, and the National Geographic Society's 1998 expedition ended with the death of the kayaker Doug Gordon. In January and February 2002 an international group made the first descent of the upper gorge.

The main tributaries are the Nyangchu, the Lhasa, the Nyang and the Parlung Tsangpo; the Nyang is the longest. In November 2020 the chairman of PowerChina announced the start of a hydroelectric project on the river. In December 2024 China approved the construction of the Medog Hydropower Station, intended as the largest hydropower dam in the world, at a cost of about 1 trillion yuan. Construction began on 19 July 2025. India and Bangladesh raised concerns about its effects in their countries.
yaroslav-ii-of-vladimir: Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, baptised Theodore, was born on 8 February 1191, the fourth son of Vsevolod the Big Nest and Maria Shvarnovna. In 1200 his father sent him to rule Pereiaslav near the Kypchak steppes. Six years later the boyars of Halych summoned him to their city, but he could not claim the throne. He was then sent to take Ryazan, and the stubborn opposition of its inhabitants led to the city being burnt. In 1209 Vsevolod sent him against Mstislav the Bold in Novgorod, and after several battles the two made peace and Yaroslav married Mstislav's daughter.

On his deathbed Vsevolod left him Pereslavl-Zalessky. In the quarrel between his elder brothers Konstantin and Yuri he supported Yuri. In 1215 he accepted an offer from the Novgorodians to be their prince, but he captured Torzhok and blocked its grain from Novgorod. He was defeated by his father-in-law on the Lipitsa River, and a helmet he lost there was found by archaeologists in 1808. He returned to Novgorod in 1234, defeated Lithuanians and the Teutonic Knights some years later, and in 1236 moved to Kiev on the advice of Daniel of Galicia, leaving his son Alexander as his representative in the north.

In 1238, when the Mongols first invaded Kievan Rus' and Yuri was killed in battle, Yaroslav left Kiev for Vladimir, where he was crowned grand prince. He tried to restore the cities of Vladimir-Suzdal after the ravages of the Mongol invasion. In 1243 Batu Khan summoned him to Sarai, and after a long conference he returned with honours. Two years later Güyük Khan summoned him to Karakorum.

According to Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Yaroslav ate at the tent of Töregene Khatun, fell ill at once, and died within a week, on 30 September 1246. Carpine reports that everyone believed Töregene had poisoned him in order to conquer his lands, though later historians have disputed the accusation. By his third wife, Fedosia Igorevna of Ryazan, whom he married in 1218, he had at least twelve children, among them Alexander Nevsky, Andrei II of Vladimir, Mikhail Khorobrit, Yaroslav of Tver and Vasily of Kostroma.
yaroslav-of-tver: Yaroslav Yaroslavich was born in 1230, a son of Yaroslav II and a younger brother of Alexander Nevsky. In 1247 he received the town of Tver from his uncle. From this small appanage he and his son Mikhail presided over Tver's transformation into one of the principal centres of power in medieval Russia, which would later compete with Moscow. All the later princes of Tver descended from him.

In 1252 Yaroslav and his brother Andrey seized Alexander's capital, Pereslavl-Zalessky. Alexander, reinforced by Tatar units, fought it back, taking Yaroslav's children prisoner and leaving Yaroslav's wife dead on the field of battle. Yaroslav fled to Ladoga. In 1255 he became prince of Novgorod after Alexander's son Vasily was expelled, but Alexander returned to the city, dismissed the posadnik, and by the next year Vasily had been sent back to reign. In 1258 Yaroslav visited the khan's capital at Sarai, and two years later he led the Novgorod army against the Teutonic Knights.

When Alexander died in 1263, Yaroslav quarrelled with Andrey over who should become grand prince. They went to the Golden Horde for arbitration, which was decided in Yaroslav's favour. He nevertheless settled in Novgorod and married a daughter of a local boyar. Various Novgorodian factions still conspired against him and sought to place on the throne either his brother Vasily of Kostroma or Alexander's son Dmitri of Pereslavl.

In 1270 the armies of three princes stood for a week near the town of Staraya Russa, ready for battle, until the metropolitan managed to reconcile them. Yaroslav surrendered Novgorod to his nephew and accompanied him to Sarai. He died on his way back to Tver on 9 September 1271. His eldest son Svyatoslav succeeded him in Tver, and Svyatoslav was followed by Mikhail.
yaroslav-osmomysl: Yaroslav was the son of Volodymyrko of Halych and his wife, a daughter of King Coloman of Hungary. He married Olga, daughter of Yury Dolgoruky, and they had four children: Vladimirko, later Prince of Halych; Euphrosyne, who married Prince Igor Svyatoslavich of Chernigov in 1184; Vysheslava, who married Prince Odon of Poznan the same year; and a daughter betrothed in 1167 to King Stephen III of Hungary, who repudiated her a year later.

Yaroslav's foreign policy leaned towards alliance with the kings of Hungary and Poland and against the Grand Princes of Kiev, who backed his cousin Ivan Berladnic in attempts to seize towns on the border with Volynia. After many years of war Yaroslav secured Berladnic's expulsion to Byzantium. In 1164 to 1165 Andronikos, cousin of the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos, escaped captivity and fled to Yaroslav's court. The prospect of a bid for the throne backed by Galicia and Hungary set off a burst of Byzantine diplomacy: Manuel pardoned Andronikos, and Yaroslav was persuaded to give up his Hungarian ties. As late as 1200 the princes of Galicia served Byzantium against the Cumans.

His later years were troubled by his family. In 1172 he repudiated Olga and took as concubine a Halychian woman, Anastasia. The boyars, unwilling to accept her as queen, stirred up a rising in which Anastasia was burnt at the stake. Yaroslav swore to live in peace with Olga, but the next year sent her back to Suzdal with their son Vladimirko. He left his throne to Anastasia's son Oleg, whom the people called Nastasyich, giving Vladimirko only Przemyśl; Oleg was soon killed and Vladimirko took the whole principality.

Yaroslav died on 1 October 1187 and was buried in the Assumption Cathedral of Halych, at the present village of Krylos. In 1939 the archaeologist Jaroslaw Pasternak found his stone sarcophagus, already looted, with his bones mixed with those of a young princess; the sarcophagus is shown in the History Museum of Ivano-Frankivsk. Pasternak hid his finds from Halych before the Soviet occupation of Western Ukraine and died in Germany without revealing where. Yuriy Lukomskyy found them in 1992 in the crypt of St. George Cathedral in Lviv, where they were reburied after study and a reconstruction of the face was made.
yaroslav-the-wise: Little is known of Yaroslav's early years. He was a son of Vladimir the Great, presumably by Rogneda of Polotsk, although his age as stated in the Primary Chronicle, and as shown by the examination of his skeleton in the 1930s, would place him among Vladimir's youngest children. Some scholars have suggested that his mother was in fact Anna Porphyrogenita. In the Norse sagas he appears as Jarisleif the Lame, and his lameness was confirmed by the scientists who examined his remains.

Vladimir sent him to rule the lands around Rostov, and in 1010 he was transferred to Novgorod. There he founded the town of Yaroslavl on the Volga. In 1014 he refused to pay tribute to Kiev. After Vladimir's death in July 1015 he fought a bloody war against his half-brother Sviatopolk I, during which his brothers Boris, Gleb and Svyatoslav were killed. The Primary Chronicle blames Sviatopolk.

Yaroslav defeated Sviatopolk in 1016, lost Kiev to him and his Polish allies in 1018, and firmly established his rule there in 1019. In 1024 his brother Mstislav of Chernigov defeated him, and the two divided the realm along the Dnieper. After Mstislav's death in 1036 Yaroslav ruled the whole of it. He relied on a Scandinavian alliance, married Ingegerd Olofsdotter, daughter of the Swedish king Olof Skötkonung, in 1019, and captured Tartu in 1030, renaming it Yuryev.

To defend against the Pechenegs he built a line of forts, and after his decisive victory over them near Kiev in 1036 he sponsored the building of Saint Sophia Cathedral in 1037. In 1051 he had the monk Hilarion of Kiev made metropolitan, challenging the practice of appointing Greeks. A Rus' fleet sent against Constantinople in 1043 defeated the Byzantine fleet but was nearly destroyed by a storm. The Russkaya Pravda was probably issued during his Novgorod years.

Yaroslav's daughters married into foreign courts: Elisiv to Harald Hardrada, Anastasia to the future Andrew I of Hungary, and Anne to Henry I of France, who acted as regent for her son. Three of his sons, Iziaslav I, Sviatoslav II and Vsevolod I, reigned in Kiev in turn. He urged his sons to live in peace. His sarcophagus in Saint Sophia was opened in 1936 and again in 2009, when it was found to hold only a female skeleton, and his remains are regarded as lost.
yaroslavl: Yaroslavl stands about 250 kilometres north-east of Moscow, at the confluence of the Volga and the Kotorosl. The oldest settlement in the area lies on the left bank of the Volga opposite the Strelka, the small cape where the rivers meet, and dates from the 5th to 3rd millennium BCE. The city belongs to the Golden Ring, a group of historic towns north-east of Moscow that have played an important role in Russian history. Its urban area covers about 205 square kilometres and extends across both rivers.

Yaroslavl is counted the oldest of the surviving towns on the Volga. It was founded by Yaroslav the Wise, a prince of Kievan Rus', while he ruled the Principality of Rostov between 988 and 1010. He landed at the Strelka, a spot protected by the high banks of three rivers, and began the first Kremlin. The first recorded event there was the Rostov Uprising of 1071, which followed a famine. The city is reported to have been the capital of an independent principality from 1218, and it was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1463, formally in 1471.

Fires repeatedly damaged the city in the 16th century, and the old tradition of building in wood gave way to stone. The Spaso-Preobrazhensky monastery, destroyed in 1501, was rebuilt, and its cathedral of 1506 to 1516 is the oldest unchanged building in the city. Ivan the Terrible made several pilgrimages to Yaroslavl, and its two large monasteries gained from rich gifts from his court. In the 17th century the city was Russia's second largest, and in 1612, during the Polish occupation of Moscow, it was for a time the country's de facto capital. Trade on the Volga, and north to Arkhangelsk and east to Siberia, made it wealthy, and leather-working, textiles, fragrances and silverwork flourished.

From 6 to 21 July 1918 the Yaroslavl Rebellion, an armed attempt by conservative activists to remove the new Bolshevik authorities, was crushed by the Red Army after bombardment from artillery and aircraft. Official figures put the deaths among residents at about 600, and some 2,000 buildings were destroyed or badly damaged. Yaroslavl is the administrative centre of Yaroslavl Oblast and a centre of industry, with a population of 577,279 at the 2021 census. Its historic centre is a World Heritage Site.
yashwant-rao-holkar: Yashwant Rao was the third son of Tukoji Rao Holkar. He was educated in accountancy and could read Persian, Marathi and Urdu. On 29 January 1797 Tukoji named his eldest son, Kashi Rao, as his successor. The second son, Malhar Rao, rebelled and Yashwant Rao joined him; on 14 September the army of Daulat Rao Scindia surprised their camp, Malhar Rao was killed and Yashwant Rao fled wounded. He gathered a following that included Pindharis and Afghans under Mir Khan. Claiming to act for his infant nephew Khande Rao, he declared himself head of the Holkars in January 1799, and by April had defeated Kashi Rao's commander, the Chevalier Dudrenec.

In 1799 the widows of Mahadaji Scindia asked his help to recover Ujjain and promised him four lakh rupees; he accepted five lakh from Ambaji Ingle to betray them, and looted the city. His victory over Scindia and the Peshwa on 25 October 1802, the day of Diwali, was won at Hadapsar near Pune. The Peshwa fled to Sinhagad, and Holkar took over the administration at Pune and appointed Amrutrao as Peshwa. The British, fearing for their own territories and those of their ally the Nizam of Hyderabad, decided to restore the Peshwa under their protection.

On 8 October 1804 he marched on Delhi to gain control of the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and besieged it for more than a week, but could not overcome the defence under Colonel Ochterlony. The emperor nevertheless gave him the title Maharajadhiraja Raj Rajeshwar Alija Bahadur. He appealed to other Indian rulers to join him against the British, but Daulat Rao Scindia would not fight and others gave no direct help. He fled to the Sikh Empire, where Ranjit Singh refused a British request to arrest him.

By the treaty signed at Rajghat on 24 December 1805 the British returned his territory, accepted his dominion over Jaipur, Udaipur, Kota and Bundi and undertook not to interfere in Holkar affairs; he gave up his claims to Bundelkhand and the lands north of the Chambal. He thus avoided the subsidiary alliance imposed on other Maratha chiefs. Lord Lake resigned in protest at the abandonment of the Company's Indian allies. In a letter of 15 February 1806 Holkar wrote that he had concluded the war when he found himself abandoned on all sides. He died on 28 October 1811.
yaska: Yāska's exact century is difficult to determine, and the opinions of scholars vary. Tradition makes him the author of the Nirukta and of the Nighantu, the oldest proto-thesaurus in India. He is thought to have succeeded Śākaṭāyana, an old grammarian and expositor of the Vedas whom his text mentions. Pāṇini, who came after him, cites at least ten earlier grammarians and linguists. Nirukta, or etymology, became one of the six Vedāṅgas, the limbs of the Veda and compulsory subjects of Vedic scholarship in ancient India.

The Nirukta has three parts: the Naighantuka, a collection of synonyms; the Naigama, words peculiar to the Vedas; and the Daivata, words relating to deities and sacrifices. It sets out rules for forming words from roots and affixes and a glossary of irregular words, and it formed the basis for later lexicons and dictionaries.

Yāska defined four main categories of words: nāma, nouns; ākhyāta, verbs; upasarga, pre-verbs or prefixes; and nipāta, particles. A verb is a word in which a process (bhāva) predominates, as in vrajati, walks, and a noun one in which a thing (sattva) predominates. Where a process is treated as a whole from start to finish, he held, a verbal noun such as vrajyā, a walk, is used. Scholars have related these ideas to the modern notion of grammatical aspect. Following the lost text of Śākaṭāyana, he also defended the view that most nouns derive from verbs.

Yāska is widely regarded as the precursive founder of the discipline that became etymology in both the East and the West. His view that words are the main carriers of meaning was fiercely debated in India for twelve centuries. On one side stood the Nairuktas, atomists who followed the Nirukta and took words as the primary elements of a sentence; on the other the Vaiyākarans, grammarians following Pāṇini, holists who held that the sentence comes first and words are reached only by analysis. Philosophers of the Nyaya and Mimamsa schools and Buddhist thinkers took part in the debate.
yasmah-addu: His Amorite name was Yaśmaʿ-haddu. After the assassination of Yahdun-Lim of Mari in 1796 BCE and a successful attack on the city, Shamshi-Adad set him on its throne. He governed the south-western part of his father's kingdom, along the Balikh, Habur and Euphrates rivers, bordering the state of Yamhad and the Syrian steppe of the semi-nomadic peoples, while Shamshi-Adad held the north from Shubat-Enlil and Ishme-Dagan the south-east from Ekallatum.

His father managed his affairs closely. To seal an alliance against Yamhad he arranged the marriage with Princess Beltum of Qatna, but Yasmah-Addu kept a daughter of Yahdun-Lim as his leading wife and placed Beltum second, until Shamshi-Adad angrily made him keep her at his side. The letters accuse him of laziness, of neglecting duties such as naming a governor of Terqa and a mayor of the palace, and of idling among the women while his brother won battles. Ishme-Dagan scolded him too and offered to carry his letters to their father, perhaps to help him, perhaps to gain standing. In one letter Yasmah-Addu protested that his father had promoted him and that some servant had taken his place in his father's affections.

The letters also show his part in the campaign of 1781 BCE against the Ya'ilanum tribe. Shamshi-Adad ordered that the tribesmen with him must die that night, and Ishme-Dagan later wrote that Mar-Addu and all the sons of Ya'ilanum had been killed; Mar-Addu's severed head was brought to Yasmah-Addu. Other battles of the period show captured enemies spared. A gentler letter has Ishme-Dagan praising the dressing applied by his brother's physician and sending his own physician to learn it.

Historians' view of him rests mostly on this correspondence, and the harsh words may reflect Shamshi-Adad's strain as his new empire began to break up. Few sources mention any military action of his own. After his father's death Zimri-Lim drove him from Mari in 1775 BCE, apparently without much resistance; the sources disagree whether he fled beyond his borders or was killed.
yasovarman-i: Yasovarman was a son of King Indravarman I and his wife Indradevi. Inscriptions describe him as a wrestler able to wrestle with elephants and to slay tigers with his bare hands. His teacher was the purohit Vamasiva, a Brahman of the priesthood of the Devaraja cult, whose own guru Sivasoma was connected with the Hindu philosopher Adi Shankara.

After the death of Indravarman a war of succession broke out between Yasovarman and his brother, believed to have been fought on land and on the water of the Tonlé Sap. Yasovarman prevailed. Because his father had sought to deny him the throne, he ignored any claim through Indravarman I or through Jayavarman II and built up a family tree that linked him through his mother with the ancient kings of Funan and Chenla. Twelve stone inscriptions in different parts of the country name him as a descendant of the ruling clans of Sambhupura, Aniditapura and Vyadhapura.

In the first year of his reign he built about 100 monasteries, or ashrams, across the kingdom, each a resting place for ascetics and for the king on his journeys. In 893 he took up the Indratataka Baray, the reservoir his father had begun, and raised the temple of Lolei in the middle of it. He also led an invasion of Champa that failed, as recorded at Banteay Chmar.

The move to the new capital had several motives. The old capital was crowded with the temples of earlier kings, and a new king was expected to build his own temple, which became his mausoleum at his death. The new site also lay closer to the Siem Reap River, halfway between the Kulen hills and the Tonlé Sap. Yasodharapura was linked to Hariharalaya by a causeway, and its reservoir, the Yashodharatataka or East Baray, had dykes 7.5 by 1.8 km long. Phnom Bakheng was one of three hilltop temples of his reign, with Phnom Krom and Phnom Bok.

Yasovarman is said to have had leprosy and was called the Leper King. At his death he received the posthumous name Paramashivaloka. His wife, a sister of Jayavarman IV, bore him two sons, Harshavarman I and Ishanavarman II. The capital he founded remained the royal seat for some 600 years, and the great religious monuments of the Khmer kings, Angkor Wat among them, were later built there.
yasser-arafat: Arafat was born in Cairo on 4 or 24 August 1929, the second-youngest of seven children of Palestinian parents. His father, Abdel Raouf al-Qudwa al-Husseini, was from Gaza City and worked as a textile merchant in Cairo. His mother, Zahwa Abul Saud, whose family home was Jerusalem, died in 1933. He enrolled at the University of King Fuad I in 1944 and graduated in 1950, and by 1946 was an Arab nationalist procuring weapons to be smuggled into Mandatory Palestine. When the 1948 Arab-Israeli War began he left the university and fought in the Gaza area alongside the Muslim Brotherhood, without joining it. He later served as president of the General Union of Palestinian Students from 1952 to 1956.

After the Suez Crisis of 1956 the guerrilla forces in Gaza were expelled, Arafat among them. In 1957 he obtained a visa for Kuwait, where he met Salah Khalaf and Khalil al-Wazir, who became his top aides. In the late 1950s he co-founded Fatah, a paramilitary organisation seeking Israel's replacement with a Palestinian state, which he led from 1959. He joined the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1967 and in 1969 was elected chair of the Palestinian National Council. Fatah's presence in Jordan brought clashes with King Hussein's government, and in the early 1970s it moved to Lebanon, where it took part in the Lebanese Civil War and became a target of Israeli invasions in 1978 and 1982.

From 1983 to 1993 he was based in Tunisia, and in 1985 survived an Israeli bombing of his Tunis headquarters in which 73 people died. He shifted from open conflict to negotiation, acknowledging Israel's right to exist in 1988, and took part in the Madrid Conference of 1991, the talks that led to the Oslo Accords of 1993 and the Camp David Summit of 2000. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 with Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

After being confined in his Ramallah compound by the Israeli army for over two years, Arafat fell into a coma in late 2004 and died on 11 November 2004; the cause of his death remains the subject of speculation. Palestinians generally view him as a martyr who symbolised their national aspirations, while many Israelis regarded him as a terrorist. Palestinian rivals often denounced him as corrupt or too submissive in his concessions to Israel.
yavne: Yavne lies in the southern coastal plain, about six kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea and on the eastern border of the Yavne sand dunes. The ancient town stood on a natural kurkar hill, now the archaeological site of Tel Yavne, which excavations show to have been inhabited continuously from the Bronze or Iron Age until the British Mandate. The name appears in many English translations of the Bible as Jabneh, in Greek and Latin sources as Jamnia, and in the Ottoman and British periods as Yibna. The ancient town had a long history of wine production.

In Roman times King Herod bequeathed Iamnia to his sister Salome, and it then passed to Emperor Augustus, who ran it as a private imperial estate. In 68 CE, after Vespasian had put down the revolt in Galilee, his army took the town and garrisoned it. According to rabbinic tradition, Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai obtained Vespasian's permission to settle there and teach his disciples, and after the fall of Jerusalem his school functioned as a Sanhedrin. A supposed Council of Jamnia that fixed the Jewish biblical canon was long theorised, but current scholarship largely rejects it.

The Crusaders called the town Ibelin and built a castle there in 1141. Its namesake family, the House of Ibelin, was important in the Kingdom of Jerusalem and later in the Kingdom of Cyprus. Saladin sacked it before his army was routed at the Battle of Montgisard in 1177, and in August 1187 it was retaken and burnt. The parish church became a mosque, and a minaret was added in the Mamluk period in 1337. During the 1948 war most of the villagers of Yibna fled, and the Israeli troops that arrived on 5 June found the village almost deserted.

Modern Yavne was founded in October 1948 as a transit camp for Jews from Arab countries, Iran and Europe, and the first neighbourhood followed in early 1949. It received city status in 1986 and lies in the Central District of Israel. The minaret of the old mosque still stands, and excavations at Tel Yavne since 2005 have uncovered the gate room of the Crusader castle.
yazd: Yazd is the capital of Yazd province in central Iran, and its name means pure or holy, the city's name meaning City of the Holy One. Former names include Kath and Isatis. It has a hot desert climate and is the driest major city in Iran, with under 60 millimetres of rain a year and summer days frequently above 40 °C. Generations of adaptation to this setting gave it its wind towers, large underground rooms, cisterns called ab anbars, ice stores called yakhchals and one of the largest networks of qanats, underground water channels, in the world. It is also one of the largest cities built almost entirely of adobe.

Archaeological evidence north of the city suggests settlement from the Achaemenid period, and some scholars link the name to the Issatis that Pliny the Elder places in the Parthian Empire. Yazd gained prominence under the Sasanian Empire. Yazdegerd I (r. 399–420) established a mint there, and a chronicle of 1441 says it was re-founded by Yazdegerd II. After the Muslim conquest many Zoroastrians moved to Yazd, and by paying a levy it was allowed to stay Zoroastrian, with Islam becoming dominant only gradually.

Its isolated desert position spared it much warfare, and it was a haven for people fleeing the Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire. Marco Polo visited in 1272 and praised its trade and its silk cloth, called Yasdi. In the 14th century it was briefly the capital of the Muzaffarid dynasty and was unsuccessfully besieged in 1350–1351 by the Injuids under Abu Ishaq Inju. Under the Qajar Empire it was ruled by the Bakhtiari Khans.

The population was 529,673 at the 2016 census. Most people are Persians who speak a Yazdi accent, and most are Shia Muslims, with a Zoroastrian minority of around 1,000 in 600,000. Zoroastrian heritage includes a Tower of Silence on the outskirts and a temple fire said to have burned continuously since 470 CE. The oldest dated building is the 11th-century Davāzdah Imām mausoleum, and the Jame Mosque has the country's highest minarets. The silk and carpet trade of the past continues in textiles, ceramics and confectionery. The historic city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.
yazdegerd-ii: Yazdegerd II succeeded his father, Bahram V, in 438. The Romans had agreed in a treaty of 387 to share the defence of the Caucasus against nomadic attacks, and paid roughly 500 pounds of gold at irregular intervals, which they saw as a subsidy and the Iranians as tribute. When Theodosius II declined to continue, Yazdegerd declared war, with little success for either side. Vandal attacks on the Roman south led Theodosius to send Anatolius to the Sasanian camp, and in 440 both empires promised not to build new fortifications in Mesopotamia.

In the east the Kidarites and other groups known as Iranian Huns had long pressed the empire, and had forced Iran to pay tribute, which Yazdegerd refused. In 450 he led an expedition deep into Kidarite territory, taking forts, cities, captives and wealth. In 453 he moved his court to Nishapur and left his minister Mihr Narseh in charge of the empire. His forces first suffered a severe defeat, and the war continued for many years. He fortified Damghan as a border post.

Armenian and Syriac sources portray Yazdegerd as a religious fanatic, while Arabic and Persian sources show a pious king who clashed with the aristocracy. Persecution of Christians began in 446 with the nobles of Karkh and spread to Iberia and Armenia, and the Armenian rebellion led by Vardan Mamikonian was defeated and Vardan killed at Avarayr on 2 June 451, with heavy Sasanian losses. Afterwards religious freedom was allowed. Jews were persecuted too, reportedly with a ban on open observance of the Sabbath. Modern historians such as Eberhard Sauer and Scott McDonough doubt that he was a zealot, and McDonough suggests Zoroastrianism may have been a test of personal loyalty.

He was the first Sasanian ruler to take the title kay, linking the dynasty to the mythical Kayanians of the Avesta, and his coins read mazdesn bay kay. In the 440s he had a mudbrick defensive system built at Derbent to hold off incursions from the north, and a later chronicle credits him with refounding the city of Yazd.

He died in 457, reportedly without naming a successor, and civil war followed between his sons. Hormizd III took the throne at Ray, while Peroz fled north-east and raised an army, and their mother, Denag, ruled temporarily as regent from Ctesiphon. Peroz emerged victorious. Persian sources generally praise Yazdegerd as an astute and well-read ruler, known to Ibn al-Balkhi and Hamza al-Isfahani as Yazdegerd the Gentle, a favourable account that is tied to a policy of persecuting non-Zoroastrians, which appeased the aristocracy and the Zoroastrian priesthood.
yazdegerd-iii: Yazdegerd was the son of the prince Shahriyar and the grandson of Khosrow II, the last prominent shah of Iran. Khosrow was overthrown and executed in 628 by his own son Kavad II, who ordered the execution of all his brothers and half-brothers, including Shahriyar. A civil war of four years followed, and a plague killed half the population of the western provinces. After a succession of short-lived rulers, the magnates Rostam Farrokhzad and Piruz Khosrow allied and installed Yazdegerd, who had been hiding at Istakhr. He was crowned in the Temple of Anahita there, where Ardashir I had crowned himself four centuries earlier. Most scholars agree he was eight years old.

The boy lacked authority, and army commanders, courtiers and aristocrats fought each other in often deadly feuds. Regional governors declared independence, and the Pahlav faction in the north at first refused to mint his coins. The empire was also raided by the Göktürks in the east and the Khazars in the west. In 633 Muslim Arabs defeated a Sasanian force near Hira. In 636 the Sasanian army under Rostam was crushed at al-Qadisiyyah, and Rostam was killed. The Arabs reached Ctesiphon in 637 and occupied it, while Yazdegerd fled with the treasury to Hulwan.

He raised a new army in Media, which was defeated at the Battle of Nahavand in 642, and then fled to Isfahan and Istakhr. In 650 Abdullah ibn Aamir of Basra invaded Pars, and 40,000 defenders were reported killed. Yazdegerd moved on to Kirman and Sakastan, where his demands for taxes and his manner alienated the local governors. He sent envoys to Tang China from 638 to 648 seeking help, but the Chinese sent assistance only after his death.

Yazdegerd was killed in 651 by a miller near Merv, either for his jewellery or, according to The Cambridge History of Iran, at the instigation of the local margrave Mahoe. By tradition he was buried at Merv by Christian monks. His death ended more than four centuries of Sasanian rule and the last pre-Islamic Iranian empire, and made the conquest of the rest of Iran easier. He is remembered as a martyred prince, and many later rulers and officers of Islamic Iran claimed descent from him. The Zoroastrian religious calendar still uses the year of his reign as its base year.
yazid-i: Yazid was born in Syria; the year of his birth is uncertain and falls between 642 and 649. His father was Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, then governor of Syria and later caliph. His mother, Maysun, was the daughter of a chieftain of the Banu Kalb and, like most of her tribe, a Christian. Yazid grew up among his Kalbite kin in the Syrian Desert and, for the rest of the year, among the Greek and native Syrian courtiers of his father. In Mu'awiya's reign he led several campaigns against the Byzantine Empire, including an attack on Constantinople.

In 676 his father nominated him heir, the first hereditary succession in the history of the caliphate, and several grandees of the Hejaz, among them Husayn ibn Ali and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, opposed it.

Mu'awiya died in April 680. Husayn and Ibn al-Zubayr refused to recognise Yazid and took refuge in Mecca. Husayn left for Kufa to lead a revolt and was killed with his small band of followers in the Battle of Karbala. His death caused widespread resentment in the Hejaz. Ibn al-Zubayr declared Yazid deposed, and the people of Medina renounced their allegiance and expelled the Umayyads living in the city. Yazid sent an army of 12,000 men under Muslim ibn Uqba, which defeated the Medinans at the Battle of al-Harra in August 683. Accounts differ on whether the city was plundered. His army then besieged Mecca for several weeks from September 683, during which the Ka'ba caught fire.

Yazid continued his father's decentralised style of government, relying on provincial governors and tribal nobles. He kept officials such as Ibn Ziyad and the Christian Sarjun ibn Mansur, abandoned the raids against the Byzantines and made no new conquests. He dug a canal, known as Nahr Yazid, to improve irrigation in the Ghouta near Damascus.

Yazid died on 11 November 683 at Huwwarin in the Syrian desert, his favourite residence, and the siege of Mecca ended. The caliphate then fell into a civil war of nearly a decade. Many Muslims regard him as an illegitimate ruler and a tyrant, and for the Shia he is an epitome of evil, reviled in the Ashura processions. Modern historians take a milder view and consider him a capable ruler, though less successful than his father. The killing of Husayn contributed to the formation of Shia identity.
yazid-ibn-al-muhallab: Yazid was the son of al-Muhallab ibn Abi Sufra, a general of the Azd tribe, whose members had a strong presence in the garrison town of Basra. He began his military career under his father in the campaigns against the Azariqa Kharijites in Iran. In 702 he succeeded his father as governor of Khurasan, but the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, wary of the family's prestige and its power among the Azd troops, had him dismissed and imprisoned in 704. In 708 or 709 Yazid and his brothers escaped and found asylum in Palestine with the Umayyad prince Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik.

When Sulayman became caliph in 715 he made Yazid governor of Iraq, though the treasury was placed under the tax official Salih ibn Abd al-Rahman, who refused Yazid's lavish demands. In mid-716 Yazid had his authority extended to Khurasan, making him in practice viceroy of the eastern caliphate. He gave power almost only to men of his own Yaman faction, against the rival Qays–Mudar, and persecuted the relatives and appointees of al-Hajjaj; the conqueror of Sind, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, was tortured and killed.

In 716 he led an army of 100,000 men against the principalities of the southern Caspian coast. According to one version, he executed some 14,000 Turks taken at Dihistan, and he secured Jurjan by founding a city at modern Gonbad-e Kavus. His campaign in the mountains was turned back, and he withdrew in return for tribute. Caliph Umar II, who succeeded in 717, imprisoned him in Aleppo for failing to send on the caliph's fifth of the spoils.

When Yazid II came to the throne in 720, Yazid escaped, fearing punishment for the deaths of al-Hajjaj's family, the new caliph's in-laws. He took Basra and declared holy war on the Umayyads and their Syrian troops, winning support across the tribes and among the pious and the mawali of Basra and Kufa. On 24 August 720 the Syrian army of Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik met him near the site of Babylon; the Iraqis abandoned the field and Yazid was killed.

Many of his family were hunted down and killed, among them nine to fourteen boys executed on the caliph's order. His revolt was the last of the great anti-Umayyad uprisings in Iraq, and revenge for the Muhallabids became a rallying cry of the Yamanis of Khurasan during the Abbasid Revolution of 750.
yazidis: The Yazidis are a Kurdish-speaking endogamous religious group indigenous to Kurdistan, with small numbers in Armenia and Georgia. Scholars and Yazidis themselves disagree on whether they are a distinct ethnoreligious group or a religious sub-group of the Kurds. Yazidism took shape from a pre-Islamic Kurdish religious substratum, given its lasting doctrinal and institutional form by the reforms and teachings of Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir and his successors in the 12th and 13th centuries. Scholars have proposed several sources for the older substratum, from Indo-Iranian traditions shared with Zoroastrianism to ancient Mesopotamian religion and Hellenistic currents. Earlier descriptions of Yazidism as an offshoot of Islam have been widely given up.

Yazidis call themselves Êzidî. Some Western scholars derive the name from the Umayyad caliph Yazid I, which Yazidis reject. Other derivations link it to Old Iranian yazata or Middle Persian yazad, divine being, or to the phrase meaning God created me.

Yazidis first came into contact with the Ottomans in the early 16th century and lived as semi-independent groups within the empire. In 1516, after Selim the Grim took Aleppo from the Mamluks, the Yazidi Sheikh Izz ed-Din had himself named Emir of the Kurds there by having the Ottoman governors execute his rival Qasim Beg for treason; when he died without heirs the title returned to Qasim Beg's family.

Under Abdul Hamid II, loyalty was increasingly measured by Muslim identity, and conscription was used to push conversion. Omer Wehbi Pasha, sent to Mosul, used violence against Yazidis who would not cooperate. About 500 Yazidis died in the Shingal campaign of November–December 1892, Lalish was turned into a madrasah and sacred objects were confiscated. Refugees on Shingal mountain spread accounts of the atrocities, and a religious revival followed, with preaching of an imminent reign of justice. In 2014 the Islamic State captured Sinjar, and over 5,000 Yazidis were killed, thousands of women and girls enslaved and more than 500,000 people displaced.

Yazidi cultural practices and almost all of their orally transmitted religious traditions are in Kurmanji, though the Yazidis of Bashiqa and Bahzani speak Arabic. Yazidis marry only other Yazidis, and those who marry outside the community are expelled. Most Yazidis in the Middle East live in Iraq, chiefly in Nineveh and Duhok, in the Shekhan and Sinjar districts, where the shrine of Sheikh Adi stands at Lalish. Large communities also exist in Armenia, where 35,272 were counted in 2011, and in Germany, where over 230,000 live. Some followers of other monotheistic faiths equate the Peacock Angel with Satan, which has led to centuries of persecution of Yazidis as devil worshippers.
yazoo-river: The Yazoo is formed by the confluence of the Tallahatchie and Yalobusha rivers at Greenwood. It marks the eastern boundary of the Mississippi Delta, a broad floodplain that was cultivated for cotton plantations before the American Civil War and is still given to large-scale agriculture. The natural levees that flank the Mississippi keep the Yazoo running beside it until it joins it above Vicksburg, and hydrologists call any stream with this pattern a yazoo stream. Potamologists believe the river began as the lower course of the Ohio River.

The French explorer La Salle named it Rivière des Yazous in 1682, after the Yazoo people who lived near its mouth. The meaning of the name is unclear; one long-held belief is that it means river of death. The French, and later the Anglo-American settlers, called the surrounding country of Mississippi and Alabama the Yazoo lands, which gave its name to the Yazoo land scandal.

The river was of major importance in the American Civil War. In 1862, near Vicksburg, Confederates used the first electrically detonated underwater mine to sink the Union ironclad USS Cairo, whose last section was raised on 12 December 1964; the restored ship is displayed at the Vicksburg National Military Park. Twenty-nine sunken ships of the war lie in the river.

In 1876 the Mississippi shifted its course several miles west and left Vicksburg without a river front. In 1902 the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers diverted the Yazoo into the old riverbed, forming the Yazoo Diversion Canal, on which the port of Vicksburg still stands. Commercial navigation on the Yazoo has declined considerably since the 1990s and is concentrated on the stretch from Vicksburg to Yazoo City.
years-of-lead-italy: The Years of Lead emerged from the social unrest of the late 1960s. The turmoil was fuelled by the rapid changes of the post-war Italian economic miracle, which brought a mass exodus from rural areas and the chaotic growth of cities. The political system, dominated by the Christian Democracy in a permanent but unstable coalition, was paralysed, and expectations of reform in housing, education and social services, raised by the brief centre-left experiment of the early 1960s, went largely unfulfilled. The name Anni di piombo may refer to the number of shootings, or to the 1981 West German film released in Italy under that title, whose original title was Die bleierne Zeit (The Leaden Time).

Two currents of violence ran side by side. Neo-fascist groups pursued indiscriminate bombings and massacres, the strategy of tension, which sought to sow panic, blame the left and provoke an authoritarian coup. Far-left groups, most prominently the Red Brigades, founded in August 1970 by Renato Curcio, Margherita Cagol and Alberto Franceschini, carried out targeted assassinations, kidnappings and bombings meant to destabilize the state and inspire a proletarian revolution.

The Piazza Fontana bombing in Milan in December 1969 killed 17. In May 1974 a bomb exploded during an anti-fascist demonstration in Brescia, killing eight and wounding 102. The Red Brigades kidnapped and murdered the former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978. In 1980 the neo-fascist Nuclei Armati Rivoluzionari carried out the Bologna massacre, which killed 85 people and was the deadliest single attack of the era. Active armed organizations grew from 2 in 1969 to 91 in 1977 and 269 in 1979.

Between 1968 and 1988 the conflict caused 428 deaths and about 2,000 injuries. Violence declined in the early 1980s after the arrest of key terrorists and Red Brigades leaders and the introduction of anti-terrorism laws that encouraged militants to become state witnesses, the pentiti. The last killing by the Red Brigades in this period was that of Senator Roberto Ruffilli on 16 April 1988; in October hardliners declared the war against the State over. Parliamentary inquiries later revealed the involvement of rogue elements in the intelligence services and of the secret Propaganda Due masonic lodge in the strategy of tension. A link with NATO's stay-behind network Gladio was speculated but never proved in court.
yeha: Yeha lies in the northern Central Zone of Tigray, in Ethiopia. Its name is written yiḥa in Ge'ez and yḥʾ in Old South Arabian script, and the town likely served as the capital of the pre-Aksumite kingdom of Dʿmt. The settlement is also a monastery site, so it has been a place of worship for a very long time, under more than one faith.

The Temple of Yeha, the oldest standing structure in Ethiopia, is a tower built in the Sabaean style. It has been dated, by comparison with ancient structures in South Arabia, to around 700 BCE. No radiocarbon test has been made on samples from the site, but local inscriptions support the date.

David Phillipson attributes the tower's excellent preservation to two things: the care with which its builders set a level foundation firmly on uneven bedrock, and its rededication, perhaps as early as the sixth century CE, as a Christian church. Two other sites lie at Yeha. Grat Beal Gebri is a ruined complex with a portico 10 metres wide and two sets of square pillars, and a graveyard holds several rock-hewn shaft tombs, first investigated in the early 1960s. One authority has speculated that one of these tombs held a royal burial. Another believes the ancient residential area lay about a kilometre east of the modern village.

An Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church monastery stands at Yeha, founded, according to tradition, by Abba Aftse, one of the Nine Saints. Francisco Álvares visited in 1520, calling the town Abbafaçem, and described the tower, the monastery and the church. The present church shows Aksumite architectural features and was built between 1948 and 1949. Theodore Bent and his wife Mabel explored the site briefly in February 1893. Excavations began in 1952 under the Ethiopian Institute of Archeology, were interrupted under the Derg, and resumed in 1993 with a French team.
yekuno-amlak: Yekuno Amlak came from an old Amhara family and ruled locally in Geshen and Ambassel, around the Lake Hayq region, where he was educated at the Istifanos Monastery. He came from Bete Amhara, in parts of present-day Wollo and northern Shewa. Medieval texts written in support of his dynasty claimed that he descended in the male line from the royal house of Aksum, which was itself said to descend from the biblical King Solomon. On that basis his dynasty claimed that he restored a Solomonic line and cast the Zagwe kings as usurpers. His descendants kept up the claim, and the 1955 Ethiopian constitution enshrined it.

Later hagiographies say that Tekle Haymanot raised him and helped him depose the last Zagwe king; earlier ones name Iyasus Mo'a, the abbot of Istifanos. G. W. B. Huntingford explains the difference by the later rise of Debre Libanos over Istifanos. Neither tradition is contemporary with the people involved. Tradition adds that the Zagwe king Za-Ilmaknun imprisoned him on Mount Malot, and that he escaped, gathered support in the Amhara provinces and Shewa, and defeated the Zagwe king at the Battle of Ansata. Taddesse Tamrat argued that this king was Yetbarak, while Getatchew Mekonnen Hasen names Na'akueto La'ab.

As emperor he is said to have campaigned against the Kingdom of Damot, south of the Abbay River, and he founded Ankober as an alternative capital near the Emirs of Harar, with whom his relations were friendly. He wrote to the Mamluk Sultan Baibars in 1273 asking for a new Abuna for the Ethiopian church; a letter survives, and it suggests the request was not his first. E. A. Wallis Budge states that he exchanged letters with the Byzantine Emperor Michael VIII and sent him several giraffes.

Yekuno Amlak died on 19 June 1285. He is credited with building the Church of Gennete Maryam near Lalibela, which contains the earliest surviving dateable wall paintings in Ethiopia. His descendant Emperor Baeda Maryam I had his body reburied in the church of Atronsa Maryam. He was the founder of the Solomonic dynasty, which remained in power until 1974.
yellow-river: The Yellow River, or Huang He, is the second-longest river in China and the sixth-longest in the world, an estimated 5,464 kilometres long with a drainage basin of 795,000 square kilometres. It rises in the Bayan Har Mountains and flows generally eastwards, makes the 1,500-kilometre Ordos Loop through Inner Mongolia, turns south to form the border between Shanxi and Shaanxi, turns east again at its confluence with the Wei River and crosses the North China Plain to the Bohai Sea. It is named for the yellow colour of its water, from the sediment it carries from the Loess Plateau. Chronicles indicate that the river, once simply called the river, became muddy sometime between 367 BCE and 165 CE.

The basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese civilisation. According to traditional historiography the Xia dynasty originated on its banks around 2100 BCE, and Sima Qian's Shiji records that the Xia were founded after the tribes around the river united to fight its floods. One estimate counts 1,593 floods in the 2,540 years between 595 BCE and 1946, and the river has been nicknamed both China's Pride and China's Sorrow.

In 602 BCE it shifted several hundred kilometres east at Suxu Mouth, the first major course change recorded in history. In 1128 Song troops under the Kaifeng governor Du Chong breached the southern dikes to stop the advancing Jin army, and the river shifted south of the Shandong Peninsula into the Yellow Sea, where it flowed until 1855, merging with the Huai River. Between 1851 and 1855 it returned north, amid floods that provoked the Nien and Taiping Rebellions, and it more or less adopted its present course in the flood of 1897.

Floods of the river have killed over one million people in all. Among the deadliest were the flood of 1344 under the Yuan dynasty, the flood of 1887, which killed between 900,000 and 2 million people, and the flood of 1931, which killed an estimated 1 to 4 million and is the worst recorded flood by deaths. Flooding in 1898 left whole communities in Shandong destitute and, with the drought that followed, contributed to the rise of the Boxer movement. About 120 million people live in the basin, which holds 13 per cent of China's cultivated land.
yellow-sea: The Yellow Sea is a marginal sea of the Western Pacific. Excluding the Bohai, it extends about 960 km from north to south and about 700 km from east to west, with an area of approximately 380,000 km2 and an average depth of only 44 m; its maximum depth is 152 m. It is a section of continental shelf that was flooded after the last glacial period, some 10,000 years ago, when sea levels rose by 120 m.

Its innermost bay, the Bohai Sea, receives the Yellow River, the Hai River and the Liao River. The Korea Bay, its north-eastern extension, receives the Yalu, the Chongchon and the Taedong. Sand and silt from these rivers, together with sand storms, give the water its golden-yellow colour. The sea is one of four named after colour terms, the others being the Black, Red and White Seas. Koreans call it the West Sea, one of three seas around the peninsula.

Chinese, Korean and Japanese ships have fished its waters for centuries. The bottom layers are rich in fish, and about 200 species have been exploited commercially, among them sea bream, croakers, prawns, cutlassfish, squid, eel and Pacific herring. Navigation is another traditional activity, and the coasts are densely populated, at about 250 inhabitants per square kilometre.

The sea has a cold, dry winter, with strong northerly monsoons from late November to March, and a wet, warm summer with frequent typhoons between June and October. In the north, drift ice and continuous ice fields form and hinder navigation between November and March. Tides are semidiurnal and run higher on the Korean side, from 4 to 8 metres, than on the Chinese coast, where the range is about 0.9 to 3 metres. The fastest tidal currents, up to 20 km/h, occur in the Myeongnyang Strait between Jindo Island and the Korean Peninsula.

Near Jindo, tidal variation opens a land passage 2.9 km long between Jindo and Modo islands for about an hour, twice a year, in early May and mid-June. A local festival has long marked it, though it was little known abroad until 1975.

The main Chinese ports on the sea are Dalian, Tianjin, Yantai, Qingdao, Tangshan and Qinhuangdao. The major South Korean ports are Incheon, Gunsan and Mokpo, and North Korea's is Nampho, the outport of Pyongyang. The Bohai Train Ferry gives a shortcut between the Liaodong Peninsula and Shandong.

The southern part, including the whole west coast of Korea, holds a belt of intertidal mudflats 10 km wide with an area of 2,850 km2. They are the most important site for migratory birds on northward migration in the East Asian–Australasian Flyway. Spotted seals are the only resident seal species, and a sanctuary for them lies at Baengnyeongdo.
yellow-turban-rebellion: By 184 the central government of the Han dynasty was weakened by court eunuchs who abused their power over the emperor to enrich themselves. Corruption was seen as the cause of plagues, natural disasters and poor harvests, a sign that the emperor had lost the Mandate of Heaven. Flooding along the Yellow River drove farmers south, and the surplus of labour encouraged exploitation.

The rebels followed the Way of Supreme Peace, led by Zhang Jue and his younger brothers Zhang Bao and Zhang Liang, who had founded a Taoist sect in what is now Shandong and were praised as healers who treated poor patients free of charge. They held that an apocalyptic change would come in the jiazi year, the start of a new sexagenary cycle. Their slogan said that the Azure Sky was dead and the Yellow Sky would rise, which gave them the colour of their headwear.

A few days before the planned rising, one of the sect's founders, Tang Zhou, betrayed the plot, and the organiser Ma Yuanyi was arrested and executed in Luoyang. In March 184 Zhang Jue began the rebellion with roughly 360,000 followers, calling himself the Lord General of Heaven. The rebels attacked government offices, pillaged villages and seized commanderies, and within ten days the rising had spread across China.

Han forces under Huangfu Song, Zhu Jun and Lu Zhi fought the main rebel armies. By the start of 185 the rebellion had mostly been suppressed, and in mid-February the emperor changed his era name to Zhongping, meaning pacification achieved. Remnants rose again for two decades. The White Wave Bandits appeared in 188, and in 192 hundreds of thousands of Yellow Turban remnants who entered Yan Province surrendered to Cao Cao, who made the best of them into the elite Qingzhou Army.

The rebellion destroyed major government buildings, killed high officials and fragmented the dynasty's territory. Rebel deaths numbered in the hundreds of thousands, and many civilians were left homeless or destitute. The court's weakness and the rising political influence of regional military governors who helped suppress it led to warlord dominance and the Three Kingdoms period. After Emperor Ling died in 189, Dong Zhuo took control of the young heir and the capital, and the Han dynasty collapsed completely by 220. The revolt also marks an important point in the history of Taoism, and it is the inciting event of the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
yelu-chucai: Yelü Chucai was born on 24 July 1190 near Zhongdu, the capital of the Jin dynasty, a descendant of Yelü Bei of the Khitan Yelü clan. His father, Yelü Lu, rose from translator to minister under Emperor Zhangzong of Jin but died when his son was two, and his scholarly mother saw to his education. Offered a post in the Jin civil service at seventeen through his father's rank, he chose instead to sit the imperial examinations and came first, and by 1213 he was prefect of Kaizhou.

By the time of the 10-month Mongol siege of Zhongdu in 1213 he had been recalled to the city with the title of Auxiliary Secretary of the Boards of Right and Left. The siege caused him a mental crisis, and from 1215 he studied Chan Buddhism under Wansong Xingxiu for three years while serving as a scribe to the new rulers.

In 1218 he was summoned to the Mongol court between the Tuul and Kherlen rivers. Genghis Khan told him he had avenged the Liao on the Jin, and Yelü Chucai answered that his father and grandfather had served the Jin and that he could not count his sovereign and his father as enemies. The khan was impressed by the reply and by the tall, long-bearded man, called him Urtu Saqal, Long Beard, and took him into his retinue as scribe-secretary and court astrologer. He helped arrange Genghis Khan's meeting with the monk Qiu Chuji.

Under Ögedei Khan he was put in charge of tax reform in North China in 1229 and made head of the Great Imperial Secretariat. He separated civil from military powers and argued that an empire might be conquered on horseback but could not be ruled on horseback. When some Mongol commanders urged the razing of Kaifeng and the killing of its people, he persuaded the Mongols to rule and tax them instead. He used his office to shield Confucian scholars and to find them posts as officials and tutors to the princes.

He died on 20 June 1244, during the regency of Töregene Khatun, still treated with respect. He was buried by Kunming Lake in Beijing, where a temple to his memory stood until Red Guards razed it in 1966 during the Cultural Revolution. He is the last person recorded as able to speak the Khitan language and read the Khitan large and small scripts.
yelu-dashi: Yelü Dashi was a minor member of the imperial Yelü clan of the Liao dynasty and an eighth-generation descendant of the Emperor Taizu of Liao. His courtesy name was Zhongde. The History of Liao describes him as well versed in Khitan and Chinese scripts, excellent at riding and archery, and a graduate of the highest imperial examination in 1115. In the dynasty's last years he held increasingly important administrative and military posts, including the governorship of Taizhou and Xiangzhou.

The Jurchens established the Jin dynasty in 1115 and allied with the Song dynasty against the Liao; by 1122 the Jin held much of Liao territory. After the Liao emperor Tianzuo fled west, his uncle Prince Yelü Chun formed the short-lived Northern Liao at Liao Nanjing, now Beijing.

Under Dashi and Xiao Gan, the Liao army repelled Song attacks, but the Jin took the city in 1123. Dashi was captured, escaped after five months and rejoined the emperor. When Tianzuo planned to attack the Jin, Dashi thought it folly and in 1124 led a band of officials northwest to the garrison town of Kedun. Tianzuo was captured in 1125 and the Liao dynasty ended.

On 13 March 1130 Dashi set out west with fewer than 20,000 men and established a base on the Emil River. The ruler of Qocho welcomed him, but an attack on Kashgar in 1131 failed. In 1132 his followers proclaimed him Gurkhan. In 1134 he deposed the Eastern Karakhanid ruler of Balasaghun, Ibrāhīm II, and made it his capital. He took control of what is now Xinjiang and in May 1137 defeated a Western Karakhanid ruler at Khujand.

In 1141 Dashi met the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan and won a decisive victory. Sanjar barely escaped, and his wife was captured. Seljuk power declined sharply, and Khwarazm and the Karakhanids became vassals of the Qara Khitai. Dashi died in 1143, and his empress Xiao Tabuyan became regent. His dynasty lasted until Kuchlug usurped it and Genghis Khan conquered its lands in 1218. His victory and his good relations with Nestorian Christianity led to his link with the legend of Prester John, first chronicled by Bishop Otto of Freising in 1145.
yelu-deguang: Born on 25 November 902, before the Liao state was founded, Yelü Deguang was the second son of the Yelü clan chieftain Yelü Abaoji and his wife Shulü Ping. In 922 his father made him Generalissimo of All Forces and put him in charge of raids on the Former Jin; in 923 his troops took Ping Prefecture and defeated the Huxun tribe of the Xi. After the campaign of 926 against Balhae, Abaoji made his elder son Yelü Bei king of the new Dongdan Kingdom and gave Deguang the title of Generalissimo Crown Prince and charge of the capital Linhuang.

As emperor he honoured his mother as empress dowager and was said to be so devoted to her that he would not eat when she was too ill to eat. In 930 he named his younger brother Yelü Lihu crown prince, and Yelü Bei, passed over again, fled to the Later Tang. When Shi Jingtang, military governor of Hedong, rebelled in 936 and asked for help, offering to serve him as a father and to cede Lulong Circuit and the prefectures north of the Yanmen Pass, Taizong agreed. He made You Prefecture a southern capital to govern the sixteen prefectures, modelled his government on Chinese states and made Zhao Yanshou chancellor.

Relations soured after Shi Chonggui succeeded in Later Jin and wrote to him as grandson, not subject; Liao merchants were arrested and killed at Kaifeng. Taizong invaded in 944 but was held at the Yellow River crossing at Majiakou, and his troops slaughtered captured Han civilians. In 946 a feigned defection by Zhao Yanshou drew the Later Jin army north, where Taizong surrounded it at Zhongdu Bridge and won its commanders Du Wei and Li Shouzhen over with a promise of the throne. The capital, left undefended, surrendered.

Taizong declared himself emperor of China, broke his promises to Zhao and Du, and sent Shi Chonggui into exile as the Marquess of Fuyi. Han rebellions spread, and after he left Daliang the Yellow River ford of Heyang fell. He blamed three errors: taking money from the circuits, letting his soldiers forage, and keeping the military governors from their posts. He died on 18 May 947. His sons included Yelü Jing, later Emperor Muzong.
yemelyan-pugachev: Pugachev was the youngest son of a small Don Cossack landowner and was born in the stanitsa of Zimoveyskaya, in present-day Volgograd Oblast. He enlisted at 17, married a Cossack girl, Sofya Nedyuzheva, within the year, and joined the Russian army in Prussia during the Seven Years' War. He returned home in 1762 and reached the Cossack rank of khorunzhiy. At the siege of Bender in 1770, during the Russo-Turkish War, he first showed a flair for impersonation by telling comrades that his sword was a gift from his godfather, Peter I.

In 1770 he left the army and became a fugitive. He was arrested and escaped several times, spent time among the Cossacks of the Terek, and returned to Russia in the autumn of 1772 with the help of Old Believers. He settled near present-day Volsk and probably heard there of the rebellion of the Yaik Cossacks.

The idea of posing as the dead Emperor Peter III came to Pugachev early. Peter III had been overthrown and murdered in 1762 by supporters of his wife, the future Catherine II. Pugachev promised to restore privileges to the Cossacks and the Old Belief, and in 1773 he began an open revolt, proclaiming an end to serfdom. His army overran much of the region between the Volga and the Urals, and he gained the support of industrial peasants in the Urals. He set up a College of War with four judges to organise his army, and it paid wages and bounties to the Cossacks. His chief success was the capture of Kazan in 1774, where the city was burned to the ground.

General Pyotr Panin was slow to act against him, because of transport difficulties and indiscipline among his poorly paid soldiers. In August 1774 General Michelsohn crushed the rebels near Tsaritsyn, and about ten thousand were killed or taken prisoner. Panin carried out savage reprisals after the capture of Penza. On 14 September 1774 Pugachev's own Cossacks handed him over at Yaitsk.

Alexander Suvorov had him placed in an iron cage and sent to Simbirsk and then to Moscow. He was executed publicly in Bolotnaya Square on 21 January 1775, beheaded and then quartered. Catherine II had been trying to reform the provincial administration, but the horrors of the revolt made her drop other reforms, in particular attempts to emancipate the serfs. Alexander Pushkin wrote a history of the rebellion and used it in his novel The Captain's Daughter (1836).
yemen: Yemen lies in southern Arabia and covers 455,503 square kilometres, with a coastline of about 2,000 kilometres. It borders Saudi Arabia to the north and Oman to the northeast, and its territory includes the Socotra Archipelago and several Red Sea islands, among them the Hanish Islands, Kamaran and Perim. Socotra lies east of the Horn of Africa and is geographically and bio-geographically associated with Africa.

The country divides into four main regions: the coastal plains in the west, the western highlands, the eastern highlands and the Rub' al Khali in the east. The Tihamah, a very arid and flat plain along the Red Sea coast, ends abruptly at the escarpment of the western highlands. These highlands are heavily terraced and receive the highest rainfall in Arabia, from about 760 millimetres a year at Taiz to over 1,000 millimetres at Ibb.
