Arriving reserves turned the tide on the Golan from 8 October, and Israel pushed on towards Damascus. Jordan and Iraq sent forces to support Syria. In Sinai an Israeli force under Ariel Sharon crossed the Suez Canal at Deversoir, where a gap had been found between the Egyptian Second and Third Armies, and moved to encircle the Third Army. The Soviet Union airlifted 12,500 to 15,000 tons of supplies to its allies from 9 October. Resolution 338 of the Security Council demanded a ceasefire on 22 October, but fighting continued, and a second ceasefire took effect on 25 October.

After President Nixon authorised $2.2 billion in arms for Israel, Saudi Arabia declared an embargo against the United States, which led to the 1973 energy crisis. Kissinger pressed Israel not to destroy the trapped Third Army, hoping to draw Egypt away from Soviet influence. The war was a direct antecedent of the Camp David Accords of 1978 and the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty of 1979, and the last Israeli troops left Sinai on 26 April 1982.

Israel lost between 2,521 and 2,800 killed. The shock to Israelis was severe, since the army had grown complacent after 1967. Historians differ over whether the outcome was an Israeli victory, an Egyptian victory or a stalemate.
yonago: Yonago lies in the far west of Tottori Prefecture and faces the Sea of Japan to the north and Lake Nakaumi to the northwest. It adjoins Shimane Prefecture and stands across the lake from the Shimane capital of Matsue. The city limits are mostly flat, with the Hino River flowing through the Yonago Plain, while the southern part is hilly country at the foot of Mount Daisen. An irrigation canal called the Yonekawa carries water from the Hino River to Sakaiminato. The name is written with two kanji, meaning rice and child.

The area belonged to the ancient province of Hōki. According to the Kojiki, the tomb of the creator kami Izanami lies on the border of Yonago with Izumo Province, and many remains of the Yayoi and Kofun periods have been found within the city limits.

In the early Edo period the Tokugawa shogunate appointed Nakamura Kazutada daimyō of the 175,000 koku Yonago Domain, and the castle was reconstructed. The centre of the modern city grew from the castle town. After Nakamura died without an heir the domain was abolished and its lands passed to the Ikeda clan of Tottori Domain, who kept the castle and gave it to their hereditary senior retainers of the Arao clan, who ruled it until the Meiji Restoration.

The town of Yonago was established in Aioi District in October 1889, under the new system of municipalities. A post office opened in 1872, a prison in 1877 and a courthouse in 1884, and railway services began in 1902. Yonago became a city on 1 April 1927 and absorbed the neighbouring town of Yodoe on 31 March 2005.

Yonago is the second largest city of Tottori Prefecture after Tottori and the commercial centre of its western part. Most of its workforce is employed in services, and Tottori University has a campus there. Its National Historic Sites include the ruins of Yonago Castle, the Mukoeyama Kofun Cluster, the Mukibanda Yayoi remains and the Kamiyodo temple ruins. Kaike Onsen, on Miho Bay, is said to be the birthplace of the triathlon in Japan. The city is twinned with Baoding in China and Sokcho in South Korea.
yonezawa: Yonezawa lies in the southeast corner of Yamagata Prefecture and covers 548.51 square kilometres. Its southern and eastern parts are river basins surrounded by large mountains, forming the Yonezawa Basin, and the Mogami River flows through the city. The south has complex terrain of several rivers and alternating ridges and valleys running east to west. Part of the city lies within the Bandai-Asahi National Park. The climate is humid continental, with warm to hot summers, cold winters and heavy precipitation from August to October.

The area was part of ancient Dewa Province and was controlled in the Sengoku period by the Date clan. The warlord Date Masamune was born in Yonezawa. In the Edo period the area became Yonezawa Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate, ruled by the Uesugi clan. After the start of the Meiji period it was organized into Minamiokitama District, Yamagata Prefecture.

Yonezawa is best known for its local delicacies, among them apples, Yonezawa beef and carp, and as a castle town that was once home to the Uesugi clan, including the daimyō Uesugi Yozan. Its economy rests on agriculture, horticulture, light manufacturing and tourism. Local attractions include Yonezawa Castle, Tateyama Castle, the Yonezawa City Uesugi Museum, Namegawa Great Falls and the hot springs of Shirabu Onsen and Yonezawa Onsen. Yamagata University has a campus in the city. Natives include the architect Itō Chūta, the statesman Hirata Tosuke and the admirals Yamashita Gentarō and Chūichi Nagumo.
yongle-emperor: Zhu Di was born on 2 May 1360, the fourth son of Zhu Yuanzhang, who in 1368 founded the Ming dynasty as the Hongwu Emperor. On 22 April 1370 he was made Prince of Yan, with his fief at Beiping, the present Beijing, and in April 1380 he moved there. In the 1380s and 1390s he proved a skilled military leader. After the Hongwu Emperor's death, the new Jianwen Emperor's advisors set out to limit the power of the princes, removing five of them, and regarded Zhu Di as the most dangerous.

In 1399 Zhu Di rebelled in the civil war known as the Jingnan campaign. He began with 100,000 soldiers and only the area around Beiping, but his troops were of higher quality. He ascended the throne on 17 July 1402 and took the era name Yongle. He erased the Jianwen Emperor's reign from the record, and tens of thousands of people were purged, among them Huang Zicheng and Qi Tai, who were put to death with their families and followers.

He made Beiping, renamed Beijing in 1403, a second capital, and its construction between 1407 and 1420 employed hundreds of thousands of workers. He had the Grand Canal rebuilt to feed the capital and the northern armies, finishing in 1415. He sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia, which employed about two thousand scholars. Unlike his father, he avoided frequent purges. He led five campaigns into Mongolia, which failed to secure the northern border, and annexed Đại Việt in 1407 as Jiaozhi Province. In 1405 he appointed the eunuch Zheng He admiral of a fleet whose voyages reached India, Hormuz, Arabia and East Africa.

On 1 April 1424 the emperor set out on his last campaign into Mongolia, which failed. He died on 12 August 1424 at Yumuchuan, and private records suggest that a series of strokes killed him. He was buried in the Chang Mausoleum, the first of the Ming tombs north of Beijing, and his son Zhu Gaochi succeeded him as the Hongxi Emperor. Historians such as Chan Hok-lam, Edward Dreyer and Frederick Mote have described his reign as the second founding of the Ming dynasty.
yongle-encyclopedia: The Yongle Emperor, known for his military achievements, was also a reader who wished to categorize literary works into a reference encyclopedia to preserve rare books and simplify research. He raised the standing of the Hanlin Academy, which had handled clerical tasks such as drafting edicts, by selecting only top recruits and leaving clerical duties to imperial officers. In 1404, a year after the commission, a team of 100 scholars led by Xie Jin finished a manuscript called A Complete Work of Literature, but the Emperor rejected it and insisted on more volumes. In 1405 the number of scholars rose to 2,169, and they were sent across China to find books. The monk Yao Guangxiao was general editor.

The work was completed in 1408 at the Guozijian in Nanjing and filled 11,095 volumes, occupying about 40 cubic metres, with 370 million Chinese characters. It was meant to include every commentary written on the Chinese classics and all history, philosophy, arts and sciences, as a collation of excerpts and works from the whole of Chinese literature. It was handwritten, not printed, on special paper and bound in the wrapped-back style, with red ink, reserved for the emperor, for titles and authors. Entries were ordered by the sounds of characters under the Hongwu zhengyun, not by subject. Non-Confucian scholars wrote the Buddhist, Daoist and divination sections, and some Neo-Confucians dismissed the work as wheat and chaff.

The encyclopedia stood in Nanjing until 1421, when the capital moved to Beijing and it went to the Forbidden City. It narrowly escaped a fire in 1557, and the Jiajing Emperor had a manuscript copy made between 1562 and 1567. The original was lost afterwards, and theories include its burning in 1644, burial with the Jiajing Emperor, and the Qianqing Palace fire. Most of the copy was burnt or looted when Anglo-French forces invaded Beijing in 1860; about 5,000 volumes remained in 1875 and 800 by 1894, and the Boxer Rebellion and the Hanlin Academy fire cost more. The largest holding, 221 volumes, is at the National Library of China in Beijing, and the National Palace Museum in Taipei holds 62.
yongli-emperor: Zhu Youlang was the son of Zhu Changying, the seventh son of the Wanli Emperor, and of Empress Dowager Ma. He inherited the title Prince of Gui from his brother and lived obscurely as a minor member of the imperial family until the peasant rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor killed himself at Coal Hill. Six weeks later the Manchu army entered the city and proclaimed the Qing dynasty, and over the next two years the loyalist Hongguang, Longwu and Shaowu emperors were captured and executed in quick succession.

Zhu Youlang became Caretaker of the State on 20 November 1646, after the death of the Longwu Emperor. When Longwu's brother proclaimed himself emperor as Shaowu, Youlang took the throne on 24 December 1646 with the era name Yongli, meaning perpetual calendar; their brief civil war ended a month later when the Qing captured and executed Shaowu. For his first five years his adoptive mother, Empress Dowager Wang, acted as his adviser, and it was said that he followed her wishes in everything.

Qing pressure drove the court from Guilin in Guangxi to Jiangxi and Hunan, then to Nanning. Youlang came to rely on local warlords and bandit chieftains, the most effective of whom, Li Dingguo, enlarged Southern Ming territory in the south-west for five years. The Qing answered by placing the region under the former Ming official Hong Chengchou as governor-general of five provinces, and by 1658 Youlang had been forced back into Yunnan.

Pindale Min, king of the Taungoo dynasty of Burma, allowed him to live at Sagaing, near Ava, if his men gave up their weapons. Fighting soon broke out between the exiles and their hosts; after Pye Min overthrew Pindale in May 1661, he ordered the Chinese followers killed, sparing only Youlang. In December 1661 Wu Sangui entered Burma with 20,000 men and demanded the emperor, and on 22 January 1662 he and his sons and grandsons were sent by boat to Wu's camp. Taken to Yunnanfu, he was strangled by Wu Sangui in June. Zhu Shugui, Prince of Ningjing, performed rites in his name in the Kingdom of Tungning until 1683.
yongzheng-emperor: Yinzhen, the future Yongzheng Emperor, was born on 13 December 1678, the eleventh recorded son of the Kangxi Emperor and the fourth prince to survive into adulthood. His mother, a court attendant of the Manchu Uya clan, was of low status and had no right to raise her own children, so Noble Consort Tong raised him. Kangxi gave his sons a rigorous education and took them on inspection trips; Yinzhen was made a beile in 1689 and a junwang, a prince of the second rank, in 1698.

In 1712 Kangxi deposed Yinreng a second time and named no heir, which set his sons against one another. Yinzhen had supported Yinreng, built his own base of support largely out of the limelight, showed no ambition and pleaded for mercy for other princes. When Kangxi died in December 1722 Yinzhen took the throne. Kangxi's choice was known only through a testament provided by Longkodo, and no decisive evidence showed it was not fabricated, so rivals such as Yinti, Yinzhi and Yinsi opposed him.

In 1723 he adopted the era name Yongzheng, "Harmonious Justice", and it has been suggested that the second character was meant to cover his disputed claim. Much of his early reign went on purging dissidents, and he grew increasingly fearful that his brothers would plot against him.

Nian Gengyao, commander of the Qing army in Xinjiang, was demoted and forced to take poison in 1726. Immediately after his enthronement Yongzheng cracked down on corruption and debt, relying partly on a secret report system in which trusted informants wrote privately to the emperor. He made meltage fees on silver an official source of local income, grouped the merchant houses of Canton into the Cohong in 1725 and removed all foreign priests from China. When civil war tore Tibet in 1727-1728 he intervened and left a Qing Resident, the amban, and a garrison.

Yongzheng ruled for thirteen years and died suddenly in 1735, aged 56, while reading court documents. It is likely that he died of poisoning from an elixir of immortality he was taking, and his successor, the Qianlong Emperor, evicted all Taoist priests from the palace. His reign was much shorter than those of his father and his son but achieved important reforms. Many consider it authoritarian, some calling him a benevolent despot and others holding that his autocratic policies went too far.
york: York lies in the Vale of York, a flat area of fertile arable land bordered by the Pennines, the North York Moors and the Yorkshire Wolds. The city was built at the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss on a terminal moraine left by the last ice age. It grew up as a river port, and the Ouse was originally a tidal river accessible to the seagoing ships of the time. The Roman name Eburacum or Eboracum is a Latinisation of a Brittonic word that may mean place of yew trees, or alternatively property of a man named Eburos.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Mesolithic people settled in the area between 8000 and 7000 BCE. By the time of the Roman conquest the land was held by a tribe the Romans called the Brigantes, whose territory first became a client state. Its leaders later grew hostile, and the Ninth Legion was sent north of the Humber into it. The city was founded as Eboracum in 71 CE. It became the capital of Britannia Inferior, a province of the Roman Empire, and was later the capital of the kingdoms of Deira and Northumbria and of Scandinavian York.

In 1068, two years after the Norman invasion, the people of York rebelled. The rising succeeded at first, but William the Conqueror suppressed it on arriving and at once built a wooden fortress on a motte. After a second rebellion in 1069 he built another timber castle across the Ouse. Both were destroyed in 1069 and rebuilt about the time of his ravaging of Northumbria, the Harrying of the North, when he destroyed everything from York to Durham.

York declined economically in the Tudor period. The Dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII ended its monastic houses. This contributed to the Pilgrimage of Grace, an uprising of northern Catholics, and Henry restored his authority by setting up the Council of the North in the dissolved St Mary's Abbey. The railway promoter George Hudson brought the railway to York in 1839, and the city was a major railway centre by the late 19th century.

York is a cathedral city in North Yorkshire, the traditional county town of Yorkshire. Its minster, castle and city walls are all Grade I listed. The walls are the most complete in England and incorporate part of the Roman fortress wall. York Minster is a large Gothic cathedral, and the Jorvik Viking Centre and the National Railway Museum are among the city's museums.
york-factory: York Factory stands on the north bank of the Hayes River, about 11 kilometres inland from the southwestern shore of Hudson Bay and some 200 kilometres south-southeast of Churchill. The much larger Nelson River, which drains Lake Winnipeg, reaches the sea just to the north, but the Hayes was the more practical canoe route. The bay was too shallow for seagoing ships to come close, so they anchored at Five Fathom Hole and smaller boats carried goods to the post.

The Hudson's Bay Company first set up Fort Nelson at the mouth of the Nelson River and then built York Factory on the Hayes, naming it after the Duke of York. New France contested the bay. Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville was driven off in 1690, captured the post in 1694 and renamed it Fort Bourbon, lost it the next year, and took it again in 1697 after winning the Battle of Hudson's Bay. The French held it until the Treaty of Utrecht returned it to the British in 1713.

For its first century the depot drew First Nations traders to it rather than sending traders out, until competition from the voyageurs of the North West Company pushed the company to build inland posts as far as the Oregon Country. From 1821 to 1873 York Factory was headquarters of the Northern Department, and from 1821 to 1846 the York Factory Express travelled twice a year to Fort Vancouver.

A stone and brick fort called the Octagon, built from 1788 to 1795, could not withstand the heaving permafrost and was razed in 1831, the year the present wooden building's centre was finished. By the mid-19th century the settlement had 50 buildings, though few liked it: the trader John McLean left in 1837 with little regret for its fogs, bogs and mosquitoes. Its role shrank after Rupert's Land passed to Canada, and in 1929 Churchill, joined to Winnipeg by rail, took its place.

The company closed the post in 1957, and its Cree residents were moved to York Landing, Split Lake and Shamattawa; Cree elders have recalled their wish to stay at Kihci-waskahikan, the Great House. Designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1936, it has belonged to the Canadian government since 1968 and is run by Parks Canada. Its building of 1831 is the oldest and largest wooden structure built on permafrost in Canada.
york-maine: York lies on the Atlantic coast near the southern tip of Maine, on the Gulf of Maine, in York County. Its first name, Agamenticus, is an Abenaki term for the York River that was also given to the hill, visible from sea, now called Mount Agamenticus, whose summit stands 692 feet (211 metres) above sea level. The town is divided into the villages of Bald Head, York Village, York Harbor, York Beach and Cape Neddick, and lies about 65 miles (105 km) north of Boston.

In 1638 the settlers renamed it Bristol after the English city from which they had come. Sir Ferdinando Gorges, lord proprietor of Maine under the Plymouth patent, envisioned a great city rising from the wilderness and named the capital of his province Gorgeana. A charter from King Charles I made it the first incorporated city in America. After Gorges died, the Massachusetts Bay Colony claimed his territory, and in 1652 York was incorporated from part of Gorgeana, becoming the second oldest town in Maine after Kittery, incorporated two years before.

Control stayed contested. In 1662 the Crown ruled that Massachusetts Bay had exceeded its charter, and a royal commission visited in 1664. On 14 July 1668 John Leverett and Richard Waldron led twelve cavalrymen into York, deposed the officials and swore in new ones on the authority of Boston.

The first Congregational church was organised in 1672 under Shubael Dummer. In the Candlemas Massacre of 1692, during King William's War, Abenaki raiders destroyed York. Dummer was shot at his own front door, about 50 people were killed and nearly 100 were carried away captive. The last local attack came at Cape Neddick in 1723, during Dummer's War. Hostilities lessened after the French defeat at the Siege of Louisbourg in 1745 and ended with the Treaty of Paris of 1763. As provincial capital and site of the Royal Gaol, York prospered on trade with the West Indies, shipping lumber and farm goods for sugar and molasses; the merchant John Hancock kept a warehouse there. Jefferson's Embargo Act of 1807 crippled this trade.

After the Civil War, York's sea breezes and colonial houses drew tourists, and it became a fashionable summer resort, like Bar Harbor and Newport, with Gilded Age buildings in the Shingle style. Buildings in York Village are kept as museums by the Old York Historical Society. The Cape Neddick Light at Nubble Rock is among its best-known sights. The population was 13,723 at the 2020 census.
york-minster: A bishop of York was summoned to the Council of Arles in 314, which points to a Christian community in York at that time, though archaeological evidence for Christianity in Roman York is limited. The first recorded church was a wooden structure built hurriedly in 627 to baptise Edwin, King of Northumbria. Its location and that of its successors before 1080 are unknown. It was probably in or beside the old Roman principia, the military headquarters, and so near the present minster but not directly on the same site. Excavations in 1967-73 found no remains of the churches before 1080.

A song school was founded in 627 by Paulinus of York, the first Archbishop of York, and choir schools have been associated with the minster since the 7th century. The undercroft of the present building contains re-used fabric of about 1160.

York Minster is the seat of the archbishop of York and the mother church of the diocese and province of York. It is the second-largest Gothic cathedral of northern Europe and charts the development of English Gothic architecture, with Early English transepts, a Decorated nave and chapter house, and a Perpendicular eastern arm and central tower. Most of the building dates from between 1220 and 1472, and it is built of creamy magnesian limestone quarried at Tadcaster. It has a cruciform plan, an octagonal chapter house attached to the north transept and a central tower 72 metres high.

The minster keeps most of its medieval stained glass. The Dean and Chapter commissioned John Thornton in 1405 to design the Great East Window, for which he was paid £66. Its scenes come from the Book of Revelation, and it is the largest expanse of medieval stained glass in the country. The north transept holds the Five Sisters window, five lancets of grisaille glass.

Thomas Becket's shrine at Canterbury made it a rival draw for pilgrims, and York responded by seeking a saint of its own. On 18 March 1226 Pope Honorius entered the name of William Fitzherbert, a former archbishop, among the saints. In 1279 his remains were moved to a shrine behind the high altar, and King Edward I helped carry the chest.

On 9 July 1984 a serious fire damaged the south transept, and firefighters deliberately collapsed its roof to save the rest of the building. The heat shattered the glass of the rose window, but the lead held it together so that it could be taken down and restored. The 311 panels of the Great East Window were removed for conservation in 2008, and a renovation of the east front begun in 2007 was completed in 2018. An astronomical clock installed in the north transept in 1955 commemorates airmen killed in the Second World War.
yorkshire: Yorkshire takes its name from the city of York, being York's shire. The name York is believed to come from the Brittonic Eburākon, probably meaning place of yew trees, which became Eboracum to the Romans, Eorfowīc to the Angles and Jórvík to the Vikings. The south-west includes Leeds, Sheffield, Bradford, Doncaster and Wakefield, and Hull lies in the south-east. The North York Moors fill the north-east, the Vale of York the centre, and the Pennines, including the Yorkshire Dales, the west. The historic boundaries were reasonably stable from 1182, when western areas went to the new county of Lancashire, until 1889.

By the late Iron Age the area was held by British Celtic tribes, the Brigantes in the north and west and the Parisi in what is now the East Riding. After the Romans left, small kingdoms arose, among them Deira in the east, Ebrauc around York and Elmet in the west. In 1066, shortly before the Battle of Hastings, Harold II marched north and defeated Tostig and Harald Hardrada of Norway at Stamford Bridge, where both were killed. Many castles, among them Richmond, Pickering, Skipton and York, were built in the Norman period.

In the Wars of the Roses, between the houses of York and Lancaster, battles were fought at Wakefield and Towton, the latter called the bloodiest ever fought on English soil. In the 16th and 17th centuries the wool textile industry moved from cottage work in the old market towns to mills in the West Riding powered by Pennine streams, helping Wakefield, Halifax, Leeds and Huddersfield to grow, while coal mining first came into prominence.

The county was divided into three ridings, East, West and North, a word of Viking origin from Threthingr, a third. Each was divided into wapentakes. York became a county corporate in 1396 and Hull in 1440, independent of the ridings. Each riding had its own lord-lieutenant from 1660, and from 1889 to 1974 the ridings were administrative counties.

Yorkshire's culture draws on Celts, Romans, Angles, Norse Vikings and Normans, and its dialect has roots in Old English and Old Norse. The white rose, once the badge of the Plantagenet House of York, is its emblem, and Yorkshire Day is observed on 1 August. York Minster is the largest Gothic cathedral in northern Europe.
yoshida-shoin: Yoshida Shōin was born Sugi Toranosuke in Hagi, in the Chōshū region, the second son of a modest-ranking samurai, Sugi Yurinosuke. At the age of four he was adopted by Yoshida Daisuke, whose house taught military studies to the daimyō, and he became heir of the Yoshida line at five when Daisuke died. His uncle Tamaki Bunnoshin hurried his education, and at eleven he impressed the daimyō Mōri Takachika with a lecture.

In 1851 he went to Edo and studied Western military science under Sakuma Shōzan, and at the end of that year he left on a four-month journey through north-eastern Japan without written permission. For this offence of dappan, fleeing the domain, he lost his samurai status and his stipend of 57 koku.

Allowed back to Edo in January 1853, Shōin saw the Black Ships of Matthew Perry at Uraga with Sakuma Shōzan and was deeply impressed by Western civilization. He first tried to board a Russian warship at Nagasaki, but it sailed early. In 1854 he followed Perry's fleet to Shimoda and, with Kaneko Shigetske, rowed a stolen fisherman's boat out to the USS Powhatan on 27 March.

He was refused and handed to the authorities. His automatic death sentence was reduced after the intervention of Kawaji Toshiakira and two senior councillors. In the Noyama Prison at Hagi he lectured fellow prisoners on the Analects and Mencius and wrote a Record of Imprisonment.

Released into house arrest in 1855, he began lecturing in a small room of the Sugi house in 1856. In 1857 he took over the Shōkasonjuku Academy, which his uncle had run. His students included Kusaka Genzui, Takasugi Shinsaku, Itō Hirobumi and Yamada Akiyoshi, and since he could not travel, he sent them round Japan as investigators. In 1858 the shogunate signed a treaty without imperial sanction. Shōin proposed seizing the senior councillor Manabe Akikatsu on his way to Kyoto, killing him if he refused to act, but most of his disciples opposed it. He was imprisoned again.

Moved to Edo during the purge directed by the Tairō Ii Naosuke, Shōin confessed to the plot before the Council of State and was sentenced to death. He was beheaded on 21 November 1859, aged 29. Of his students, Takasugi Shinsaku led rifle companies against the shogunate's army in 1864, and Itō Hirobumi became Japan's first prime minister; Katsura Kogorō, Inoue Kaoru and Yamagata Aritomo also became known. He was enshrined in Setagaya in 1882, at Hagi, and at Yasukuni Shrine in 1888.
yoshino-nara: Yoshino (吉野町, Yoshino-chō) is a town in Yoshino District, in the central part of Nara Prefecture. The Ryumon Mountains run east to west in the north, the Omine Mountain Range spreads out to the south, and mountains extending from the Daidaka range lie to the east. Between them the Yoshino River flows from southeast to west through the centre of the town, and the Takami River flows from east to west. Settlements lie on the narrow stretches of flat land inside the meanders of the Yoshino River and on the more open land along its tributaries. The climate is humid subtropical, with an average annual temperature of 13.0 °C and about 1,893 millimetres of rain a year.

The area was part of ancient Yamato Province. The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki mention Yoshino as a stopover on Emperor Jimmu's eastward journey to conquer Yamato. In the Asuka period, because it lay directly south of the capitals Asuka-kyō, Fujiwara-kyō and Heijō-kyō, it was a popular recreational spot for Emperor Ojin and other emperors and aristocrats, and Yoshino Palace stood there. During the Nara period the area was sacred to adherents of Shugendo. It was the capital of the Southern Court in the Nanboku-chō period.

After the Meiji restoration the village of Yoshino was established on 1 April 1889 under the modern municipal system. It became a town on 24 April 1928 and on 3 May 1956 annexed the town of Kamiichi and the villages of Kokusui, Nakasho, Ryumon and Nakaryumon. A local story holds that Prince Oama, later Emperor Tenmu, taught the people of the Kuzu district to make washi paper in the 7th century.

Mount Yoshino is known for its many thousands of cherry trees, which have inspired poetry by Chiyo, Uejima Onitsura and other writers. They were planted in four groves at different altitudes so that they come into bloom at different times in the spring. An account written about 1714 describes about 1,000 trees at the base, 1,000 in the middle, 1,000 higher up and 1,000 in the precincts of the inner shrine at the top.

The town has 5,874 people and covers 95.65 square kilometres. Its economy is based on forestry, sake brewing and tourism, and most of its forest is red cedar and cypress that have been planted and harvested in cycles for 500 years. Kinpusen-ji, Kinpu Shrine, Yoshino Shrine and Yoshino-Kumano National Park lie within it. In 2012 it was designated one of the Most Beautiful Villages in Japan.
young-italy: A few months after leaving Italy, in June 1831, Giuseppe Mazzini wrote a letter to King Charles Albert of Sardinia asking him to unite Italy and lead the nation. A month later, convinced that his appeal had not reached the king, he founded the movement at Marseille, in July 1831, while in exile. Its goal was a united Italian republic, to be won by a general insurrection in the reactionary Italian states and in the lands held by the Austrian Empire, since Mazzini believed that a popular uprising would create a unified Italy.

Its slogan was Union, Strength and Liberty. Members took nicknames from figures of the Italian Middle Ages and swore an oath to make Italy united, free, independent and republican, with every man considered equal.

The movement gathered about 60,000 members around 1833. In that year members plotting a revolt in Savoy and Piedmont were arrested and executed by the Sardinian police, and in Austria links with the movement were treated as treason, punishable by death. After a second failed revolt in Piedmont and Savoy in February 1834 it disappeared for a time, then reappeared in England in 1838.

Later insurrections in Sicily, Abruzzi, Tuscany, Lombardy-Venetia, Romagna (1841 and 1845) and Bologna (1843) failed. The short-lived Roman Republic of 1848 was crushed by a French army called in by Pope Pius IX, whom Mazzini had first hailed as a likely leader of liberal unification.

Giuseppe Garibaldi joined around 1833 after meeting Mazzini, took part in a failed revolt in Piedmont and was sentenced to death, and fled to Marseille. Young Italy became affiliated with Giovine Europa, founded in 1835, alongside similar movements such as Junges Deutschland, Młoda Polska and Giovine Svizzera. A last failed revolt against Austria in Milan in 1853 effectively ended it.

The failure of the Milan revolt of 1853 crushed hopes of a democratic Italy and favoured the Piedmontese monarchy, which achieved national unification in 1860 under Count Cavour. Young Italy inspired Mlada Bosna, an early 20th-century Serbian revolutionary movement in occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, and similar youth nationalist movements in Asian and African colonies from the mid 19th century to decolonisation.
young-ottomans: The society grew from a picnic in the Belgrad Forest near Istanbul in the summer of 1865, where six young men, Mehmed Bey, Namık Kemal, Menâpirzâde Nuri, Kayazade Reşat Bey, Ayetullah Bey and Refik Bey, formed the group that became its nucleus. Almost all of them had worked in the Translation Bureau of the Sublime Porte and knew both European political systems and Ottoman foreign policy. Within two years a few hundred people had joined, among them Prince Murad and Prince Hamid, nephews of the Sultan.

In 1867 Namık Kemal and others published the open letter of the Egyptian prince Mustafa Fazıl Pasha to Sultan Abdülaziz calling for constitutional and parliamentary government. The government cracked down, and the members fled to Paris, where under the prince's patronage they began calling themselves Yeni Osmanlılar. Their papers, among them Hürriyet, published by Namık Kemal and Ziya Pasha from 1868, appeared in London, Geneva, Paris, Lyon and Marseille.

After the deaths of Mehmed Fuad Pasha in 1869 and Mehmed Emin Âli Pasha in 1871 many exiles returned, but the group fractured: Ali Suavi resigned and Ziya Pasha moved to Geneva. Drought and floods in Anatolia in 1873 and 1874, the stock market crash of 1873, revolts in the Balkans and war with Russia from 24 April 1877 gave them an audience. Murad V, installed after the coup of 30 May 1876, was declared unfit to rule after three months, and Abdul Hamid II prorogued parliament on 13 February 1878.

The group held no single ideology, but its members shared a constitutionalism grounded in Islam and the idea of Ottoman patriotism. Namık Kemal's poems and his play Vatan (Fatherland) urged all Ottomans to put devotion to the fatherland above loyalty to their religious communities, the beginning of territorial patriotism. The Young Ottomans are regarded as the first modern ideological movement among the Ottoman elite and the first to use the press to shape public opinion, and by giving new meanings to words such as vatan and hürriyet they lent their language to later nationalist and liberal groups.
youth-pledge: The first Indonesian youth congress met in Batavia, capital of the Dutch East Indies, in 1926. It took no formal decisions but promoted the idea of a united Indonesia. The mood was tense, as the Dutch colonial authority had just crushed a joint rising of communists and religious groups in Cilegon, Banten, and West Sumatra. At the first congress Mohammad Yamin drafted a pledge whose third part named the language of unity as Malay. Mohammad Tabrani objected that it should be Indonesian, so that each part of the formula ended with the name Indonesia, and no agreement was reached.

Yamin's proposal came before the second congress, held on 27 and 28 October 1928 in three places. The first session, in the Katholieke Jongelingenbond building, voiced the hope that the congress would inspire a feeling of unity, and the second, in the Oost Java Bioscoop building, discussed education. The third and final session met at Jalan Kramat Raya 106, a house owned by Sie Kong Lian. Wage Rudolf Supratman played his song Indonesia Raya on the violin while Theodora Atia "Dolly" Salim, daughter of Haji Agus Salim, sang it, the words modified slightly so as not to provoke the Dutch. The congress closed with the reading of the pledge.

The decision, officially titled the Decision of the Congress of Indonesian Youth, was first written in the Van Ophuijsen spelling of the time. In it the sons and daughters of Indonesia acknowledge one motherland, Indonesia; acknowledge themselves to be of one nation, the nation of Indonesia; and uphold the language of unity, the Indonesian language. The final wording thus kept Tabrani's change, and the second congress is taken to mark the birth of the Indonesian language. By Presidential Decree No. 316 of 16 December 1959, 28 October became a national day, though not a public holiday.
ypati: Ypati lies about 25 km west of Lamia and 30 km west of Thermopylae, overlooking the valley of the Spercheios, with forests and grasslands on the higher ground to the south. About 3 km to the north-west are the hot springs, now Loutra Ypatis, which Herodotus records and which were visited in antiquity. The ancient name, Hypate or Hypata, probably comes from hypo Oita, near Mount Oeta.

Founded in the late 5th or early 4th century BCE as the capital of the Aenianes and their league, the town came under Macedonian rule around 344 BCE and joined the Aetolian League about 273 BCE. The Roman general Manius Acilius Glabrio ravaged it in 191 BCE, and in 168 BCE Rome restored the league of the Aenianes with Hypata as its capital. Under Augustus it took the name Hypata Augusta, and by the 2nd century CE it was counted the most important city of Thessaly; a local family whose members mostly bore the names Cyllus and Eubiotus led the league and funded the Pythian Games.

The town was probably abandoned after the Slavic invasions of the 7th century and reappeared in the 9th century as Neai Patrai, New Patras, a metropolitan see by about 900. After 1268 it was the capital of the principality of Thessaly under John I Doukas and his heirs. Nerio Acciaioli took it from the Catalans in 1391, and the Ottomans under Bayezid I three years later. It changed hands several times before the Ottomans held it for good from 1423, calling it Patracık, Little Patras.

During the Greek War of Independence rebels attacked it three times in 1821 and 1822. Ypati joined Greece in 1830 and took back its ancient name. On 17 June 1944 German troops, in reprisal for partisan attacks, executed 28 people and burned 375 of the town's 400 buildings.

Ypati is a village of about 440 people and a municipal unit of Lamia. The Greek state has declared it a martyr city. Its medieval castle, restored in 2011–15, is open to the public, and the town has the Byzantine Museum of Phthiotis, the Byzantine-era Church of Hagia Sophia and, 3 km to the west, the 15th-century Agathonos Monastery.
ypres: Ypres, officially Ieper in Dutch, is a city and municipality in the province of West Flanders, Belgium. The municipality includes villages such as Boezinge, Brielen, Zillebeke and Vlamertinge and has about 34,900 inhabitants. The town is known to have been raided by the Romans in the first century BCE, is first mentioned by name in 1066, and is probably named after the river Ieperlee, on whose banks it was founded.

In the Middle Ages Ypres was a prosperous Flemish city with 40,000 people in 1200, known for its linen trade with England. As the third largest city of the County of Flanders after Ghent and Bruges, it played an important part in the textile industry, and its cloth reached Novgorod in the early 12th century. The Cloth Hall was built in the 13th century. A fire in 1241 ruined much of the old city, and during the Norwich Crusade of Bishop Henry le Despenser it was besieged from May to August 1383 until French relief forces arrived. It became the seat of a new diocese in 1561.
Forces of Louis XIV took it on 25 March 1678, and Vauban built the fortifications still visible. It passed to the Habsburgs in 1713, and the French captured it again in 1794.

In the First World War Ypres stood in the path of the German sweep into France from the north. The Germans surrounded it on three sides and bombarded it for much of the war, while British, French and allied troops made costly advances from the Ypres Salient. In the Second Battle of Ypres, which began on 22 April 1915, the Germans used poison gas for the first time on a large scale, chlorine, and mustard gas was first used near the town in autumn 1917. The Third Battle of Ypres, or Passchendaele, from 31 July to 10 November 1917, brought nearly half a million casualties to all sides for only a few miles gained. The town was all but obliterated.

After the war Ypres was rebuilt with German reparations, its main square, Cloth Hall and town hall as close to the originals as possible. Britain decided in September 1920 that the Menin Gate would be a memorial, and it was unveiled on 24 July 1927; it names Commonwealth soldiers who fell in the Salient and have no known grave. Since 1929 the Last Post has been sounded there each evening at eight o'clock, apart from the German occupation of the Second World War, when it was held at Brookwood Military Cemetery in England. The Cloth Hall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, houses the In Flanders Fields Museum, and the Cat Parade is held every three years.
yser: The Yser has a course of 78 kilometres, of which about 30 are in France. It has two official sources, at Buisscheure and Lederzele, west of Cassel in the department of Nord, and passes Bollezeele and Bambecque before entering Belgium. It then flows through Diksmuide and reaches the North Sea at Nieuwpoort by the Ganzepoot lock complex. Its basin covers 1,101 square kilometres, two thirds of it in Belgium. The name IJzer is of Celtic origin, like that of the Isar in Germany, the Jizera in Bohemia and the Isère in France, since the Celtic Menapii lived in the area before Roman times.

In the Middle Ages the land between the Yser and the coast was Veurne-Ambacht. At the end of the 16th century it came into Spanish hands, and settlements and forts were built along the river against plundering by reformers from Ostend. They largely lost their function after the fall of Ostend in 1604. After the Peace of Aachen the area around Veurne passed to France, and the Yser formed a northern border of the French realm, with fortifications such as Fort Knokke. After the Treaty of Utrecht it belonged to the Austrian Netherlands, and the river gradually lost its role as a border.

In the First World War the Yser lay on the front line, with the Belgian and German armies dug in on either side. During the Battle of the Yser in 1914 part of the polder west of the river between Nieuwpoort and Diksmuide was flooded with seawater by opening the sluices, an obstacle to the advancing German army that kept the westernmost part of Belgium free of occupation. The inundation was made at the suggestion of the investigating judge of Veurne, with the cooperation of Karel Cogge and Hendrik Geeraert. The river itself never overflowed its banks.

The Belgian army held the line for the rest of the war, and monuments such as the Yser Tower and the Death March at Diksmuide recall it. In May 1940 the French and British allies blew up the bridges and locks again.
yu-the-great: Transmitted sources agree that Yu was the son of Gun, though they differ on Gun's origins. According to Sima Qian's Shiji, Gun was a mere official and Yu's descendant line ran back through Zhuanxu to the Yellow Emperor. Gun was enfeoffed at Shiniu of Mount Wen, in modern Beichuan County, Sichuan, where Yu is said to have been born, although Shifang is also named. When Yu was a child Emperor Yao made Gun Earl of Chong, and Yu is believed to have grown up on the slopes of Mount Song. He married a woman of Mount Tu, and they had a son, Qi.

An excavated manuscript, probably of the Warring States period, tells a different legend of his birth: his mother conceived by eating Job's tears grains and bore him through her back after three years.

In Emperor Yao's reign floods plagued the Chinese heartland. Gun spent more than nine years building dikes and dams, to no effect. Yu studied the river systems, and with Hou Ji devised a system of irrigation canals that led flood water into fields, while dredging the riverbeds over thirteen years. He is said to have opened the narrow channel at Mount Longmen, known since as Yu's Gateway. Tradition says he passed his own door three times in those years without going in, and that his hands and feet were thickly calloused.

Emperor Shun, impressed by his work, passed the throne to Yu rather than to his own son. Yu is said to have declined at first and to have accepted at age 53. He founded the Xia, traditionally China's first dynasty, with a capital at Anyi. According to the Book of Documents he divided the Chinese world into nine zhou, or provinces, and cast the Nine Tripod Cauldrons from bronze received from them.

According to the Bamboo Annals, Yu ruled for forty-five years; he is said to have died of an illness at Mount Kuaiji, south of present-day Shaoxing, and to have been buried there. The Yu Mausoleum, first built in the 6th century, stands four kilometres southeast of the city, and emperors, notably Qin Shi Huang, travelled there for ceremonies.

No contemporary evidence for Yu exists, and his name first appears on vessels of the Western Zhou, about a thousand years after his traditional date. Early 20th-century scholars of the Doubting Antiquity School proposed that he began as a water god or beast. Later he was regarded as an ideal ruler, and in Taoism and Chinese folk religion as a water deity.
yuan-dynasty: The Yuan was a Mongol-led dynasty and a successor state of the Mongol Empire after its division. Genghis Khan became Great Khan in 1206, and under his son Ögedei the Mongols destroyed the Jin dynasty in 1234, conquering most of northern China. Kublai, unable to read Chinese, had Han teachers from his early years and sought the counsel of Chinese Buddhist and Confucian advisers. After Möngke Khan granted him control of the Mongol territories in China, he built schools for Confucian scholars, issued paper money and revived Chinese rituals.

In 1271 Kublai issued the Proclamation of the Dynastic Name, naming the dynasty Great Yuan and claiming succession to the Chinese dynasties from the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to the Tang. He placed Genghis Khan in the imperial records as official founder, with the temple name Taizu.

The early years were unstable. Kaidu, a grandson of Ögedei, refused to submit, and the Song dynasty remained an obstacle in the south. Kublai installed the hostage prince Wonjong as ruler of Goryeo in 1259, making it a tributary, and suppressed the revolt of Li Tan in 1262. The conquest was complete in 1279, when the Southern Song fell at the Battle of Yamen.

Succession was a lasting problem. Kublai's eldest son Zhenjin died in 1285, and Zhenjin's third son ruled as Temür Khan from 1294 to 1307. Elective kurultais were held until 1311, but after 1320 they were a formality, and real power over succession lay with empress-dowagers, guard units or high officials. The final years brought struggle, famine and bitterness among the populace. In 1368 the Ming dynasty defeated the Yuan forces, and the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau, where the Northern Yuan lasted until 1635.

The population was divided into four classes: Mongols, the Semu from western and Central Asia, the Han, mostly former subjects of the Jin, and the Nan or Southerners, subjects of the Southern Song, who stood at the bottom of the privilege ladder. The imperial examinations were not restarted until 1315. Tibetan Buddhism became the de facto state religion, and the ʼPhags-pa script, invented in 1269, was used to write Mongolian, Tibetan and Chinese. Underglaze blue and white porcelain began at Jingdezhen in the early 14th century.
yuan-shao: Yuan Shao, courtesy name Benchu, was born in Ruyang County in Runan Commandery. His family had held high positions in the Han civil service for over four generations, and he was a great-grandson of Yuan An. His birth was a source of dispute with his half-brother Yuan Shu, since his mother had been a servant of Yuan Feng; the Records of the Three Kingdoms hold instead that he was an older cousin adopted by Yuan Cheng. Yuan Shao helped save some of the partisans during the Disasters of Partisan Prohibitions, and he later served as an aide to General-in-Chief He Jin, who trusted him deeply.

After Emperor Ling died in May 189, He Jin and Yuan Shao plotted against the eunuchs, and He Jin summoned Dong Zhuo's troops to Luoyang. He Jin was assassinated on 22 September 189. Dong Zhuo then seized the capital, and when Yuan Shao opposed his plan to depose Emperor Shao he fled to Ji Province. In early 190 a coalition of regional officials, including Cao Cao and Yuan Shu, formed behind him.

Dong Zhuo moved the capital to Chang'an and burned Luoyang, but the coalition's leaders, disunited, soon went home. Yuan Shao took Ji Province from Han Fu in 191 and built a state at Ye, and in the winter of that year he defeated Gongsun Zan's cavalry at the Battle of Jieqiao using massed crossbowmen.

In 195 Ju Shou urged him to welcome Emperor Xian, but Guo Tu and Chunyu Qiong opposed it, and Cao Cao took the emperor to Xuchang instead. After destroying Gongsun Zan at Yijing in 199, Yuan Shao held the four provinces north of the Yellow River and allied with the Wuhuan tribes. In 200 he marched against Cao Cao with more than 100,000 veteran troops and many militia. At Guandu, Cao Cao burned his supply depot at Wuchao, officers including Zhang He and Gao Lan defected, and Yuan Shao fled north with hundreds of men. Cao Cao defeated him again at Cangting in 201.

Yuan Shao put down rebellions in his domain and restored order, but he died on 28 June 202 without choosing between his sons Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang. Yuan Shang took the succession with the support of Shen Pei, Pang Ji and Lady Liu, and the sons then fought each other. Cao Cao eliminated Yuan Shao's heirs and remnants by 207. After taking Ye in 204 he wept at Yuan Shao's tomb and gave the family gifts and a pension. His failure, despite his family and position, was commonly blamed on indecisiveness and his inability to heed his advisers.
yuan-shikai: Yuan Shikai was born on 16 September 1859 in Zhangying village, in Xiangcheng county, to an affluent Han family, and was the fourth of six sons. He received a traditional Confucian education, failed the imperial examinations twice, in 1876 and 1879, and entered public life through the Huai Army, in which many of his relatives served. In 1882 he went to Joseon (Korea) with troops sent by Li Hongzhang to restore order, and he distinguished himself on Wu Changqing's staff. He later commanded the Chinese forces there, trained the Korean royal guard, and after he thwarted the Kapsin Coup in 1885 was made imperial resident and supreme adviser to the Korean government.

Recalled to China in 1894, he was given the task of training the New Army the next year, which formed the basis of his Beiyang Army. He took an active part in the late Qing reforms, including the abolition of the imperial examination system. The Hundred Days' reformers accused him of betrayal for tipping off Ronglu about their plans, which brought him into Empress Dowager Cixi's favour. Appointed Viceroy of Zhili in 1902, he built the Beiyang Army into the best trained force in China. After Cixi's death the Prince Regent Zaifeng dismissed him.

After the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 the Qing court recalled him, and he became prime minister on 1 November. His army fought briefly against Sun Yat-sen's revolutionaries before negotiations began. Under the deal Sun would step aside in Yuan's favour if Yuan secured the abdication of the Qing court, and Yuan became provisional president of the Republic of China.

In 1913 Yuan's alleged part in the assassination of Song Jiaoren and the reorganisation loan affair provoked Sun Yat-sen's Second Revolution, which was crushed. He outlawed the Kuomintang, dissolved the National Assembly and replaced the provisional constitution. In December 1915 he proclaimed himself Hongxian Emperor, which provoked the National Protection War. Faced with widespread opposition he abdicated in March 1916 and restored the Republic, having been emperor for only 83 days. He died of kidney failure on 6 June 1916, aged 56, leaving a weakened Beiyang government and a fragmented political landscape that soon fell into warlordism.
yuan-shu: Yuan Shu, courtesy name Gonglu, was born in 155 in Ruyang County, Runan Commandery, in present-day Henan. His family had been prominent in the Han civil service for more than four generations, with members in high office since the first century CE. He was a son of the Minister of Works Yuan Feng. As a young man he gained a reputation for gallantry and liked to hunt with dogs and falcons. Nominated as Filial and Incorrupt, he became Intendant of Henan and then General of the Household Rapid as a Tiger.

After the death of General-in-Chief He Jin on 22 September 189, Yuan Shu led the Imperial Tiger Guards against the eunuch faction. When Dong Zhuo seized the Han government he fled to Nanyang Commandery, which he took over after Sun Jian killed its grand administrator. He joined the campaign against Dong Zhuo led by Yuan Shao, but when it broke up in 191 the two vied for northern China, each forming alliances. Defeated by Cao Cao and Yuan Shao in 193, including at the Battle of Fengqiu, he withdrew to Shouchun on the Huai River and built a powerful warlord state there. His rule in Nanyang had been despotic and his regime extravagant.

From 194 to early 197 Sun Ce and Wu Jing conquered much of Jiangdong on his behalf, but he fared worse in Xu Province against Liu Bei and Lü Bu. In early 197 he declared himself emperor, citing omens, among them the characters of his given and courtesy names and his possession of the Imperial Seal, which had passed to him from Sun Jian. The act made him a target of the other warlords, and many followers deserted, Sun Ce among them.

After crushing defeats by Cao Cao, Liu Bei and Lü Bu, Yuan Shu tried to flee north to join Yuan Shao. Yuan Shao sent his eldest son Yuan Tan to help, but Yuan Tan arrived too late, and Liu Bei blocked and turned back Yuan Shu's forces to Shouchun. He died soon afterwards in 199, of starvation, being unable to swallow the coarse food his soldiers ate. His last request was for honey water, which his soldiers did not have. His son Yuan Yao fled to Lujiang, was captured by Sun Ce and later worked as a Palace Gentleman in Eastern Wu; Yuan Yao's daughter married Sun Fen, a son of Sun Quan.
yucatan-peninsula: The peninsula covers approximately 181,000 km2 and has low relief, composed almost entirely of porous limestone. It is the exposed part of the larger Yucatán Platform, a flat karst landscape on the Maya Block, the southernmost part of the North American plate. It lies east of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, which some regard as the geographic boundary of Central America. The Yucatán Channel, between its north-eastern corner and Cuba, connects the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea.

The northern half has no rivers above ground. A freshwater lens floats on saline water beneath the whole peninsula, and the thousands of sinkholes called cenotes give access to it; ancient and contemporary Maya have long relied on them. The climate is tropical, semi-arid in the north-west and humid in the south, and the peninsula lies within the Atlantic hurricane belt.

The peninsula is the site of the Chicxulub crater, made 66 million years ago by an asteroid about 10 to 15 km across at the end of the Cretaceous. A ring of cenotes outlines one of the shock waves of the impact. The earliest human remains are from caves near Tulum: in 2020 divers and archaeologists excavated Chan Hol cave and found the skeleton of a woman about 30 years old who lived at least 9,900 years ago.

The peninsula makes up a large part of the ancient Maya lowlands and was a central location of Maya civilisation. Among its better-known sites are Chichen Itza, Coba, Tulum and Uxmal. In the 9th century a widespread political collapse in the central Maya region brought civil wars, the abandonment of cities and a northward shift of population, and in the Postclassic period Chichen Itza rose in the north.

The Spanish conquest of the Maya was prolonged, since the Maya kingdoms resisted integration into the Spanish Empire so tenaciously that their defeat took almost two centuries. The Caste War of Yucatán, which began in the 1840s, drove all non-natives from the region, and the independent Maya state of Chan Santa Cruz was conquered by the Mexican federal army in 1901.

The peninsula comprises the Mexican states of Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo, Guatemala's Petén Department and almost all of Belize. Maya and Mestizos make up a sizable part of the population, and Mayan languages are widely spoken. The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System stretches over 1,100 km along its eastern coast. Cattle ranching, logging, chicle and henequen were once its main products, and since the 1970s tourism has grown, above all in Quintana Roo.
yudhishthira: His name means one who is steady in battle, and he is also called Dharmaputra and Dharmaraja. According to the Mahabharata, he was born by niyoga, since a curse had made intimacy fatal for King Pandu. Pandu died in the forest and his second wife Madri ended her life, and forest sages took Kunti and the children to Hastinapura, where they were handed to Bhishma. The brothers trained under Kripa and later Drona, and Yudhishthira excelled in chariot warfare. When Duryodhana drugged and threw Bhima into the river, Yudhishthira advised his brothers to keep the matter secret and not seek revenge.

Dhritarashtra gave the Pandavas half the kingdom, the forest of Khandavaprastha, which Yudhishthira with Krishna's blessing and Vyasa's help made into the capital Indraprastha. Narada advised that Draupadi spend a year with each brother in turn, and Yudhishthira put this rule in place. For the rajasuya, Krishna suggested removing Jarasandha of Magadha, and Yudhishthira sent his brothers in four directions to subdue rival kings and gather tribute. He accepted the dice match citing the duty of a kshatriya to accept a challenge, obedience to elders and the inevitability of fate.

In exile he received from the sun god Surya the Akshaya Patra, a copper plate whose food did not run out. At a lake, a Yaksha put questions to the brothers, and the four who drank without answering died. Yudhishthira answered, and when offered one brother he chose Nakula, saying Kunti's line would live through himself and Madri's should not end, whereupon the Yaksha revived all of them. In the last year he served King Virata of Matsya in disguise as a Brahmin named Kanka. After the war he did not wish to rule, but his brothers and Bhishma persuaded him, and he reigned for 36 years and performed the Ashvamedha.

At the onset of the Kali Yuga and Krishna's departure, Yudhishthira and his brothers gave up the throne to Parikshit, Arjuna's grandson, and set out with a dog on a pilgrimage to the Himalayas towards Mount Meru. Draupadi and then each brother fell dead on the way. Yudhishthira alone ascended to heaven in his mortal body. Buddhist sources, by contrast, describe Kuru as a minor state ruled by a chieftain called Koravya of the Yuddhitthila clan.
yue-fei: Several sources state that Yue Fei was born into a poor tenant farmer's family in Tangyin County in Henan. His biography, written about sixty years after his death by his grandson Yue Ke, says that he was named Fei, meaning to fly, because a large bird like a swan landed on the roof of the house when he was born. Some later historians doubt many of Yue Ke's claims. The biography also says that he learned archery from Zhou Tong. He loved to read military classics, among them the Zuo Zhuan and the strategies of Sun Tzu and Wu Qi.

Although his literacy would have allowed him to become a scholar, he chose the military because his family had no tradition of civil service. He joined the Song army in 1122, left briefly when his father died in 1123 and returned in 1126.

After re-enlisting, Yue fought rebellious local warlords responsible for looting in northern China. He took part in defending Kaifeng during the second Jin siege in 1127. After Kaifeng fell he joined an army at Jiankang that stopped the Jurchens reaching the Yangtze in 1129. In 1133 he became general of the largest army near the central Yangtze. Between 1134 and 1135 he led a counteroffensive against Qi, a puppet state supported by the Jin, and secured territory the Jurchens had conquered.

Just as Yue threatened to retake Kaifeng, officials advised Emperor Gaozong to recall him and sue for peace. Gaozong feared that a defeat at Kaifeng might lead the Jurchen to release Emperor Qinzong, threatening his claim to the throne, and sent twelve gold plaques ordering Yue back. Yue submitted, was imprisoned, and Qin Hui arranged his execution on false charges. He died on 28 January 1142. According to his biography he tore open his jacket in court to show four characters tattooed on his back meaning serve the country with the utmost loyalty.

Yue was pardoned posthumously. Emperor Xiaozong gave him the posthumous name Wumu in 1169, and later he was made King of E. His stature as a national hero rose after his execution, strengthened in the Yuan dynasty, and temples to him were built in the Ming. Later historians blamed Qin Hui and in some accounts Gaozong. The claim that Qin Hui conspired with the Jin has never been proven. Modern accounts note that he was not the only general against the Jurchens and was not an erudite Confucian scholar, and that many exaggerations trace to Yue Ke's biography.
yuezhi: The Yuezhi are first described in Chinese histories as nomadic pastoralists living in an arid grassland in the western part of modern Gansu during the 1st millennium BCE. The Guanzi mentions nomads called the Yuzhi or Niuzhi who supplied jade to the Chinese and, unlike the neighbouring Xiongnu, did not fight nearby Chinese states. The Book of Han says the Great Yuezhi were a nomadic horde with over a hundred thousand soldiers who lived between Dunhuang and Qilian. No archaeological remains of them have been found there, and some scholars place their homeland further northwest, north of the Tian Shan. Many scholars believe they were an Indo-European people, though there is no evidence linking them to the Tarim mummies or the Tocharian languages.

After a major defeat by the Xiongnu in 176 BCE the Yuezhi split into two groups. The Lesser Yuezhi moved to the southern mountains to live with the Qiang. The Greater Yuezhi began migrating north-west about 165 BCE and settled in the Ili valley, where they defeated the Sai. In 132 BCE the Wusun, allied with the Xiongnu, dislodged them, and they passed through Dayuan in Ferghana and settled on the northern bank of the Oxus in northern Bactria.

A Chinese mission led by Zhang Qian reached them in 126 BCE to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu, but they refused, since they now lived peacefully and had no interest in revenge. Later Chinese accounts describe them as occupying Bactria in five major tribes, one of which, the Guishuang, took control of the confederation.

The Kushanas, widely believed to have been a dynastic clan or tribe of the Yuezhi, founded the Kushan Empire. At its peak, in the 3rd century CE, it stretched from Turfan in the Tarim Basin to Pataliputra on the Gangetic plain. The Kushans played an important role in the Silk Road trade and in the introduction of Buddhism to China. The Yuezhi in Bactria became Hellenized to some degree, adopting the Greek alphabet and minting coins in Greek. The Lesser Yuezhi are linked to the Yicong Hu, who helped drive the Liangzhou Rebellion of 184-221 CE, and, controversially, to the Lushui Hu, who founded the Northern Liang in 397.
yugoslav-committee: In October 1914 the Serbian prime minister Nikola Pašić learnt that Britain was weighing offers to Hungary and Italy that could cost Serbia its hoped-for outlet on the Adriatic. He sent two Bosnian Serb deputies, Nikola Stojanović and Dušan Vasiljević, to the émigrés Ante Trumbić and Julije Gazzari, proposing a body that would carry out propaganda for a South Slav union built by the expansion of Serbia. The four met in Florence on 22 November 1914. The Treaty of London of 1915, which promised Italy lands on the Adriatic inhabited mostly by Croats and Slovenes, pushed the émigrés closer to Serbia.

The committee was an unelected, ad hoc group of anti-Habsburg politicians and activists who had fled Austria-Hungary, with its seat in London. Trumbić was president and Frano Supilo vice-president until 1916; members included the sculptor Ivan Meštrović, Hinko Hinković, Gustav Gregorin and Bogumil Vošnjak. Donations from the Croatian diaspora paid for most of its work, and the Serbian government covered part. Its members disagreed on whether the new state should be centralised or federal. Supilo resigned after concluding that the Serb members wanted a centralised state, and was accused in turn of favouring Croatian interests.

At Corfu in 1917 Trumbić sought assurances that Croatia would not be left inside Austria-Hungary and that Italy would not take Dalmatia, and he opposed full centralisation; the resulting declaration left most constitutional questions for later. Relations with Pašić worsened in 1918, when the Serbian government denied the committee any legitimacy and the Entente Powers declined to recognise it as an allied body.

As Austria-Hungary broke up, the National Council of the new State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs made the committee its voice abroad. At Geneva in November 1918 Trumbić won agreement on a common confederal government, but a week later the Serbian government renounced the Geneva Declaration. Facing unrest and the Italian advance, the National Council sent a delegation to Prince Regent Alexander, which accepted unification without agreed terms. In early 1919 Dinko Trinajstić replaced Trumbić at its head; ordered to dissolve by Prime Minister Stojan Protić, the majority refused on 12 February, but the committee ceased to exist in March 1919.
yugoslav-partisans: The Kingdom of Yugoslavia was invaded from all sides on 6 April 1941, chiefly by German forces but also by Italian, Hungarian and Bulgarian formations, and the Royal Yugoslav Army surrendered unconditionally on 17 April. The leadership of the Communist Party, with Josip Broz Tito, was then in Zagreb. While the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact was in force the communists avoided open conflict with the new regime of the Independent State of Croatia, extending their underground network and gathering weapons. In June 1941 the Central Committee decided to prepare an uprising. They were the military arm of a coalition led by the Communist Party and represented by the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia, known as AVNOJ.

After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941 the Partisans began an active guerrilla campaign, and a Communist Party proclamation of 5 July called on the Serbian people to fight. A large uprising followed, later joined by the Chetniks of Draža Mihailović, and it produced the short-lived Republic of Užice, the first liberated territory in Europe. German forces suppressed the uprising by 29 November 1941. The Partisans were nonetheless a highly mobile force that the Axis offensives failed to destroy. Their stated aims were to free Yugoslav lands from the occupiers and to establish a communist-ruled state, and the Communist Party tried to appeal to the country's ethnic groups by preserving the rights of each.

Until British supplies arrived in quantity in 1944 the occupiers were their main source of arms. By late 1943 the Allies had shifted support from Mihailović to Tito as Chetnik collaboration became evident, and the Partisans were recognised at the Tehran Conference. By late 1944 they numbered about 650,000, organised in four field armies and 52 divisions, and in the autumn they and the Soviet Red Army liberated Belgrade in the Belgrade Offensive. They were also the only resistance movement in occupied Europe to use significant air and naval forces.

By the end of the war the Partisans controlled the whole country, as well as Trieste and Carinthia. After it they were reorganised as the regular armed force of the newly established Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia. Within Croatia the movement's leaders later founded the Federal Republic of Croatia as a constituent of the new federation.
yugoslavia: The idea of a common state for all South Slavic peoples emerged in the late 17th century and gained prominence through the Illyrian Movement of the 19th century. The name combines the Slavic words jug, south, and Slaveni, Slavs. After the 1917 Corfu Declaration between the Yugoslav Committee and the government of the Kingdom of Serbia, the Kingdom of Serbia merged in 1918 with the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, after centuries of foreign rule under the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy. The kingdom gained international recognition on 13 July 1922 and was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929.

On 6 January 1929 King Alexander I abolished the constitution, banned national political parties and assumed executive power; he was assassinated in 1934, and Prince Paul acted as regent. Paul signed the Tripartite Pact on 25 March 1941, and army officers overthrew him two days later, giving the 17-year-old King Peter full powers. German, Italian and Hungarian forces invaded on 6 April 1941, and the Axis powers split the country up. The Independent State of Croatia, ruled by the fascist Ustaše, persecuted and murdered around 300,000 Serbs, along with at least 30,000 Jews and Roma.

The Communist-led Partisans proclaimed a Democratic Federal Yugoslavia, and on 29 November 1945 the Constituent Assembly proclaimed a federal republic, abolishing the monarchy. Josip Broz Tito ruled from 1944 until his death on 4 May 1980. He broke with Stalin in 1948 and in 1961 helped found the Non-Aligned Movement. The country took the name Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 7 April 1963, with six republics and the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina within Serbia.

After Tito's death ethnic tensions grew. Croatia and Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991, Macedonia in September 1991, and Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence was recognised in April 1992. Wars followed, notably in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war lasted more than three years and ended with the Dayton Agreement of 14 December 1995. Serbia and Montenegro formed a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April 1992, renamed Serbia and Montenegro in 2003, and Montenegro became independent in June 2006. Serbo-Croatian has since diverged into four standard varieties, Bosnian, Croatian, Montenegrin and Serbian, and some people from the former Yugoslavia still describe themselves as Yugoslavs.
yugra: Russian chroniclers of the 12th to 17th centuries used Yugra, or Yugor Land, as a collective name for the lands and peoples east of the northern Ural Mountains, then inhabited by the Khanty and Mansi. In the early 16th century scholars such as Maciej Miechowita noted its likeness to ugry, an Old Russian name for the Hungarians, and the name of the Ugric languages rests on that assumption. The link between the two words is disputed: András Róna-Tas has connected Yugria with the 10th–11th century ethnic name Ugur.

Novgorod reached the Ob by two routes from Ustyug, one by the Sukhona, Vychegda and Usa, the other along the coasts of the White Sea and Kara Sea, and traded iron goods and textiles for furs. Yugorshchina, a trade association, was set up in Novgorod in the 14th century. Tribute was collected only by force, and chronicles record defeats, such as the campaign led by Yadrei of Novgorod in 1193. After Moscow annexed Novgorod, Ivan III sent expeditions in 1483 and 1499–1500. The 4,000-strong force of 1499, using dog and reindeer teams, is said to have taken 40 strongholds and captured 58 Khanty and Mansi princes.

The Yugrans formed three or four proto-states, among them the Principality of Pelym and the largely Mansi Principality of Konda. Allied with the Siberia Khanate, the Mansi of Pelym raided Kaigorod and Cherdyn in 1581, and the campaign of Yermak Timofeyevich in 1582–1584 followed. In 1593 the stronghold of Prince Ablegirim of Pelym was taken and a Russian fortress built in it. Moscow subdued Yugra only in the middle of the 17th century. The Mansi were baptised in numbers from the early 18th century, when Grigory Novitsky recorded the resistance of the village elder Nahratch Yeplayev; many sacred objects were later burned, though others were hidden.

The name lives on in Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug–Yugra, a constituent of the Russian Federation, and Yugoriya serves as a poetic name for the region. Yugra and the lands to its south are regarded as the place of origin of the Hungarians, whose language is the closest relative of Khanty and Mansi.
yugurs: The Yugurs, traditionally known as Yellow Uyghurs, are a Turko-Mongol people and one of the 56 ethnic groups officially recognised in China. Their own names are Sarığ yoğır in the western group and Shera yogor in the eastern. The 2020 census counted 14,706 of them, living mainly in the Sunan Yugur Autonomous County in Gansu. The Turkic-speaking Yugurs are considered descendants of a group of Old Uyghurs who fled south from Mongolia to Gansu after the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed in 840.

In Gansu those Uyghurs established the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, which lasted from 870 to 1036, with its capital near Zhangye, at the foot of the Qilian Mountains in the valley of the Ejin River. In 1037 the Yugurs came under Tangut rule. After Khizr Khoja's invasion of Qumul, residents who rejected conversion to Islam fled to nearby Dunhuang and Hunan in China proper, and these are regarded as the ancestors of the Yugurs, who have remained Vajrayana Buddhists to the present day.

In the late 16th century they adopted the Gelug order of Tibetan Buddhism under the influence of Sonam Gyatso, the third Dalai Lama. In 1893 the Russian explorer Grigory Potanin, the first Western scientist to study them, published a small glossary of Yugur words with notes on their administration and geography.

The Yugurs speak two languages of different families. About 4,600 speak Western Yugur, a Siberian Turkic language that has preserved many archaisms of Old Uyghur, and about 2,800 speak Eastern Yugur, a Mongolic language. Mongolic and Chinese are also used in the eastern provinces. Both Yugur languages are now unwritten, although the Old Uyghur alphabet remained in use in some Yugur communities until the end of the 17th century. Most Yugurs are Tibetan Buddhists.
yuksom: Yuksom, also spelt Yuksum, lies about 40 km north of Gyalshing in the Gyalshing district of Sikkim, at an average altitude of 1,780 metres. It occupies a basin-like valley surrounded by mountain ranges, at the head of Khangchendzonga National Park, the largest protected area in Sikkim. Its hills, once called Ney-Pemathang, carry forests of oak, birch, maple, chestnut, magnolia, rhododendron, silver fir, ash and alder. The name is said to mean the meeting place of the three learned monks, and the site is counted among the sacred landscapes of Demazong, the valley of rice, believed to have been blessed by Guru Padmasambhava.

Buddhism reached Sikkim from Tibet as early as the 9th century. In 1641 Lama Lhatsun Chenpo travelled from Tibet to spread the faith and was joined by two other lamas, Sempa Chembo and Rinzing Chembo, from Kham; they met at Norbugang, the place later called Yuksom. According to the tradition, they sought a fourth person from the east, found a man churning milk near present-day Gangtok, recognised his royal links with Tibet and brought him to Norbugang. There he was enthroned on a stone pedestal on a pine-covered hill and anointed with water from a sacred urn, at the age of 38.

As Chogyal, Phuntsog Namgyal set about converting the local Lepchas to Buddhism and extending his kingdom towards the Chumbi Valley, Darjeeling and eastern Nepal. From Yuksom he set up the first centralised administration, dividing the kingdom into twelve dzongs, or districts, under Lepcha governors, with a council of twelve ministers. Yuksom's time as capital ended in 1670, when his son and successor Tensung Namgyal moved the capital to Rabdentse. The Namgyal monarchy, twelve kings in all, lasted until 1975.

Yuksom is a heritage village; the 2011 census counted 364 households and 1,951 people, mainly Bhutias and Nepalese. The Throne of Norbugang and the Norbugang Chorten mark the coronation site, and Dubdi Monastery, also called the Hermit's Cell after its founder Lhatsun Namkha Jigme, stands on a hill about an hour's walk away. These sites lie on a Buddhist pilgrimage circuit with Pemayangtse Monastery, the Rabdentse ruins and Tashiding Monastery, and the village is the starting point of the trek to Mount Khangchendzonga.
yumjaagiin-tsedenbal: Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal, born Tserenpil, was born on 17 September 1916 to an unwed Dörbet mother in a banner of what is now Uvs Province. In October 1929 he and 21 other Mongolian students were chosen for a special preparatory school in Irkutsk in the Soviet Union, and in 1931 he joined the Mongolian Revolutionary Youth League. He graduated from the Siberian Financial and Economic Institute in July 1938, was noticed by the Soviet Communist Party's Central Committee on a visit to Moscow, and returned to Mongolia that September.

Recommended to the leader Khorloogiin Choibalsan by a Soviet intelligence officer, Tsedenbal joined the party in 1939 and became finance minister. In March 1940, aged 24, he was elected general secretary, the country's number-two leader, after Choibalsan had the sitting secretary Banzarjavyn Baasanjav purged; Baasanjav was executed and rehabilitated in 1957. Tsedenbal introduced the Cyrillic script for Mongolian. After Choibalsan died in January 1952 he became premier on 27 May, and in 1958 he ousted Dashiin Damba, who had held the party post since 1954, and exiled him internally.

He resisted de-Stalinization: he blocked the commission re-examining the purges, banned the film Tümnii Neg in 1963, and a statue of Stalin stood before the National Library until 1990. He expelled rivals on charges of nationalism, among them Daramyn Tömör-Ochir in 1962, after the planned celebration of Genghis Khan's 800th anniversary was cancelled, and in 1964 an "anti-party group" of three economic officials. He called the Soviet relationship one of elder and younger brother, sided with the USSR in the Sino-Soviet split, and signed a treaty in 1966 that allowed Soviet troops to be stationed in Mongolia. He built a cult of personality, awarding himself the rank of marshal in 1979.

Memory loss and dizziness troubled him from late 1973. He resigned as premier in 1974, becoming head of state. In November 1983 the new Soviet leadership judged his behaviour a liability, and on 23 August 1984 the Mongolian Politburo dismissed him from all positions, citing his health. He lived in retirement in Moscow, where he died on 20 April 1991.

In 1988 the official media began blaming him by name for the country's stagnation, and in March 1990, at the height of the democratic revolution, the party stripped him of his titles and expelled him. A decree of President Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat in 1997 invalidated that decision. A statue of him was built in 2000, and his legacy, controversial after 1990, is remembered in Mongolia as one of relatively moderate socialism.
